title: Faisal Islam: The UK's Trump trade deal no longer looks world-beating
description: While the US tariffs imposed on the UK are effectively unchanged, other countries now have a better deal.
author: Faisal Islam
content:
It has been a long road for President Donald Trump as he looks for a justification to erect a tariff wall around the US, including against key allies.
From the opioid crisis to illegal migration, then the need to bring manufacturing back to America's shores, the list goes on.
Through Trump's second term, there has been a new justification almost every month for the trade levies he is seeking to place on allies.
Some have been overturned by the courts, others by economics and some even by their own logic. And so, Trump has now turned to effectively accusing dozens of trade partners of trading in goods that have been produced using forced labour.
These are "tariffs in search of an authority", as one industry figure put it. The forced labour line shores up President Trump's tariffs against a challenge from Congress or the courts.
In practice, the levies are curiously similar by country to a previous round of tariffs imposed supposedly for completely different reasons.
The good news for the UK is that the regime effectively remains the same as before.
What has changed is that our nearest neighbours in the European Union now have a much better deal than before, and in turn are in a better situation than the UK.
While the UK and the EU each appear to have a 10% rate, the EU's is a flat rate, while the UK's will apply alongside other tariffs, in a range of goods including footwear and textiles.
The government has struck effective side deals on medicines, steel, aluminium, cars and, with the help of King Charles, whisky.
At the end of this process however the overall trade-weighted effective tariff rate for the EU (8.5%) could end up a bit lower than the UK's (6.8%).
It should not matter that much, but the help given by doing the first deal, and by post-Brexit trade freedoms, looks to have been short-lived.
The British Chambers of Commerce trade expert William Bain points to the competitive advantage for EU exporters into the US in some sectors.
The EU has secured better treatment because it has passed a ban on forced labour goods, which the UK has not.
This is not an accusation on the use of forced labour in supply chains. It is about the passing of specific legislation, mirroring the US ban on products that have used forced labour in supply chains.
US hits dozens of countries with new wave of tariffs
What tariffs has Trump introduced and why?
There should be scope for a better deal for the UK, but it raises an interesting question about whether the government will pursue an EU-style ban. This is widely seen as a backdoor way to target China, in particular for conditions in its Xinjiang province.
Last October , external the government said it "remained firmly opposed to the use of state-imposed forced labour", but that it was "considering how best to reflect this position," citing "operational and legal complexities".
Since then, the UK has welcomed imports of Chinese cars, and is exploring a services trade deal with the country. The relationship with China has been a balancing act for the government.
This is also one of the global stories of the tariff wars. As the US repeatedly changes its rationale for tariffs, the rest of the world is focused on trading with each other. For example, Canada increased its trade with the rest of the world by more than it lost from the US.
China's total dollar trade with the US is flat in the first half of this year versus last year. Across the world it is up 21%, including 14% with the EU, 11% with the UK, and 24% with Africa.
There could be pressure now to legislate for a formal ban on forced labour products. Successive governments have opted for a lighter voluntary due diligence regime.
Will the US force a change in the UK and elsewhere, and what might it offer in return?
Or the UK may opt to keep its precarious geopolitical position by sticking to its existing deals in medicines, metals and cars.

title: The Polygamist's author says women see themselves reflected in her Netflix hit
description: Zimbabwean novelist Sue Nyathi self-funded her debut novel and now asks who can afford to write at all.
author: Megha Mohan
content:
Sue Nyathi says people call her an overnight success but "the work has been put in over many years"
When Sue Nyathi sent her debut novel The Polygamist to publishers, "they thought there was no market for the book" about a married Zimbabwean man and the women he seduces, she says.
So the Zimbabwean author found her own editor, typesetter and artist, and in 2012 published 500 copies herself. It defied the publishers' predictions and became a huge hit.
It has now been adapted for Netflix and is in the top 10 of the platform's most streamed series in more than 60 countries, reaching number two in the United States. Hollywood actress Taraji P Henson said the series had her in a "chokehold" and she binge-watched all 22 episodes in a single day.
It is not, Nyathi is careful to point out, a straightforward story about polygamy. The traditional practice of polygamy is not foreign to her. Her mother's side the family was polygamous for generations.
Her grandfather, who died in 1979, had five wives, her great-grandfather had 11. Her grandmother, the first woman his grandfather married, presided as matriarch over a farm where the wives lived together, and often helped choose the newcomers herself.
Sue Nyathi's grandmother was the first wife in a polygamous marriage, a position known as an Indlunkulu
"There was no infighting, because everyone knew their place," Nyathi says. When she asked her grandmother how she made sense of it, the answer was practical - more hands to do the work, physical labour and emotional labour alike. It was open.
"Everybody knows who's who in the zoo," Nyathi explains.
Polygamy is legally recognised in Zimbabwe and South Africa if conducted under specific established customs. But what Nyathi began to notice as a young working woman in Harare in 2001 was something else entirely.
Men who were purportedly monogamous were effectively living polygamous lives with secret women and secret households. That is the polygamy of her novel, what she calls "the modernised, or perverted, version" of the practice, relying on deception instead of consent
"I'm not against polygamy," Nyathi says. "What I'm against is the lack of agency. It's wrong for the goalposts to be shifted once you're inside."
In the novel, Nyathi's heroine, Joyce, believes she has married into a union of one man and one woman, yet her husband, Jonasi, marries and sets up homes with three other women behind her back. There is no confession and no announcement; Joyce simply comes to realise, as the secrets accumulate and the women's lives intertwine, that her idea of a monogamous marriage has been a sham all along.
There is an explosive rivalry between Joyce (in white) and Matipa (in black), who both married Jonasi
The question of who holds the power to negotiate and who does not runs through the whole storyline. Jonasi is a wealthy, self-made businessman, and in a patriarchal society he makes the decisions about everything.
Although Joyce helped him build his empire, her finances are dependent on him. The same goes for a later wife, Matipa who also works for Jonasi.
As a result the women have less autonomy, which leaves them exposed. Age gaps compound the imbalance, Nyathi notes, down to the most intimate negotiations.
An HIV thread runs through the story, and if "you're negotiating safe sex, you don't have a say in a relationship with those kinds of dynamics", she says.
There are a few differences between the book and the Netflix series - on the screen, the story is moved to South Africa, is shot in the Zulu language with subtitles and Jonasi has fewer wives. And unlike the television version, the novel is narrated entirely by Jonasi's wives.
At one point, Matipa threatens to leave Jonasi, but he persuades her to stay
"I wanted to highlight women's voices," Nyathi says, to let each woman explain why she found herself in a relationship with a man who wouldn't be faithful to her. The themes resonate with many readers, she adds. Women write to her to say they see themselves in Joyce and Jonasi's other wives. Some add that they are married to a Jonasi figure and want out.
After the series aired, Amnesty South Africa circulated guidance on narcissistic abuse and what steps a woman can take.
"For some people, this is not just a series," Nyathi says. "It's their lived reality. It holds up a mirror to society."
Not everyone has welcomed the reflection though.
Kenyan civil servant Geoffrey Mosiria called for the series to be banned in Kenya, arguing that it conflates polygamy with cheating, fraud and abuse. Nyathi is unmoved. Culture evolves, she says, and practices can be diluted or corrupted and she is showing what has happened to this one.
Simply by making affluent black Africans the protagonists, she says she has opened many people's eyes. She recalls a European reader who said he had not realised that rich black Africans existed.
"We've always had this stereotypical view of what being African is, and it's always associated with poverty," Nyathi says. The series shows otherwise and, she argues, is the richer for being filmed in the Zulu language: "English doesn't carry the same cultural richness that our languages do."
Matipa (left), Joyce (centre) and Jonasi are all involved in the family company and need to find a way to work together
If there is a note of frustration in her, it surfaces around the question of who gets to write at all. Nyathi wanted to be a writer from childhood, but her parents pushed her towards a more traditional profession.
She worked in finance for almost two decades and says her time as an investment analyst taught her to see writing as both a craft and a business. While her financial career paid the bills, writing remained her passion and she wrote The Polygamist in the evenings after she had finished work. She left corporate life at the age of 40 to write full time, a few years after she had published the novel. She is now 48.
"People say, 'Oh, you're an overnight success.' Not at all," she says. "The recognition is overnight, but the work has been put in over many years, and I've made a lot of sacrifices."
Most writers, she adds, cannot live on their books, least of all in Africa. She says that often successful writers are supported by wealthy husbands, by grants, by residencies.
But those options were not available to her - a single mother who had to put her son through school, she has juggled various jobs to keep writing.
"There's a long period between when you start a book and you finish it. It could be two years, it could be eight years. How do you survive? Practically bills still need to be paid," she says. "I've walked that journey and it's erraticâ?¦ you're definitely going to have to stay in that day job.
"Writing is a luxury that most people can't afford," she says, adding that the cost is measured in the voices that are rarely heard.
She also feels an imbalance in how African writing travels. "It's easier for an African writer published overseas to gain traction. Books are traditionally sold down to us. It's hard for our work to sell upwards."
What the "Netflix effect" has given her is precisely the visibility she had never enjoyed across four novels and more than a decade of writing, often on politically charged topics.
Nyathi is now finishing the first draft of a historical novel which she has been working on for the past two years - she says the themes will resonate with many people.
As for the craft of writing, "everything starts with a story", she says, advising any woman who thinks she has a book in her and no money, to start with a pen and paper, and do it for love.
"Money should never be the motivation. The love is what will fuel you when it gets hard."

title: Why have obesity rates doubled since 1993?
description: Around seven million more adults are living with obesity than would have been if obesity rates had stayed the same as 1993.
author: Joe McFadden, Hugh Pym
content:
If England's obesity rates were still the same as 1993 there would be seven million fewer adults living with obesity.
There are 14 million adults classified as obese, despite successive governments launching 14 separate obesity strategies over the past three decades.
It's clear something isn't working, so what's behind the increase?
And can anything be done about it?
According to new analysis by the King's Fund, in 1993 15% of those aged 16 and over in England were obese, with rates achieving a record high of 30% in 2024.
Their analysis suggests obesity rates are rising fastest in 16-to-24 year-olds, with 18% classified as obese or severely obese in 2024 compared with just 6% in 1993.
Accounting for population change, this means there are now one million young adults living with obesity in England - 700,000 more than if rates had not risen over the past three decades.
Dave Buck, senior fellow for public health at the King's Fund, called this rise "clearly worrying" and says governments have "talked the talk, but not sufficiently walked the walk" in addressing obesity rates.
"This analysis shows the scale of the failure to take the necessary action on tackling this obesity timebomb," he added.
There are several factors behind the rise in obesity, including changes in eating habits and food prices over the last 30 years.
Service industry - or "white collar" jobs - take a larger share of the economy and there has been a decline in traditional manufacturing and other "blue collar" work such as manual labour.
This means more people are in sedentary office jobs so spend more time sitting down than moving around.
Food prices have also fallen since the 1990s, partly because of increased competition between the major supermarkets alongside an increase in fast food outlets and home delivery.
Buck told the BBC that these changes mean it's "far easier to over-consume or consume in ways that add to our weight".
"With things like deliveries, it's very easy and convenient now to click a button and you get a takeaway at your door, so we're making it much easier to have high fat, high salt and high sugar foods."
Takeaways high in fats, salt and sugar are more widely available in areas of high deprivation where people are at higher risk of obesity.
Less healthy foods in supermarkets are also cheaper than they were three decades ago, while there have been several cost-of-living crises in recent years.
Obesity can be a risk factor for several chronic conditions including type 2 diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, osteoarthritis and some cancers.
Reports estimate , external obesity and being overweight costs the UK economy approximately Â£126bn per year, including Â£12bn to the NHS - roughly 7% of its annual budget.
Since 1992 - the year before data on obesity in England was first collected - 14 national obesity strategies have been published.
Campaigners argue progress has been too slow and calls for further intervention have increased in recent years.
Tony Blair's government introduced a ban on junk food advertising during children's TV programmes - although some campaigners were calling for a wider ban - while Gordon Brown launched a strategy aiming to reverse the "rising tide of obesity" after becoming prime minister in 2007.
The Conservative government introduced a UK-wide levy on high-sugar soft drinks in 2018, causing several manufacturers to cut sugar levels in their products so that they fell below the levy threshold.
During his final weeks in office in 2016, then-Prime Minister David Cameron considered banning "buy one get one free" deals for unhealthy products in supermarkets and restricting TV ads for junk food and other high sugar products.
Although both Theresa May and Boris Johnson argued at times for further action, Cameron's ideas were not followed up, partly due to the pandemic which delayed plans further, and afterwards when ministers argued restrictions on such deals would be unfair on shoppers due to surging inflation.
In January this year, the Labour government introduced a ban on junk food advertising before 21:00 on television and at any time online after almost a decade of consideration.
Further plans to crack down on the sale of unhealthy food items are still yet to come into effect despite being first pledged by Labour in 2024, while a recent select committee report urged ministers to do more like stopping fast food outlets opening close to schools.
Weight loss drugs such as GLP1s are increasingly being used to treat obesity, though only adults with a BMI of at least 35 and who have at least one pre-existing weight-related health condition qualify for Wegovy on the NHS.
People with cardiovascular disease who are classed as overweight, but not quite obese, can also be given the drug, while Mounjaro has been available from specialist NHS weight-loss clinics in England and Wales since March 2025.
Many people chose to buy these drugs privately.
A new weight loss pill from Wegovy is now available to buy privately from High Street and online pharmacies in the UK - but is not yet on the NHS.
The Department of Health and Social Care says weight loss jabs are only one part of a broader plan.
It says tackling the promotion of less healthy food and drink, increasing exercise and encouraging people to eat healthier options are all important for addressing obesity.
Earlier this year , England's Chief Medical Officer Prof Sir Chris Whitty said it would be a "societal failure" if medicating people for life was our only answer to obesity.
He says the lessons are there in other countries, such as France, which have kept obesity levels stable.
Now the question is what do we want to learn?
Clarification 13 August: The original wording in our article about obesity rates amongst adults mirrored that used by the NHS and King's Fund. We changed this section to make it clearer to readers that the figures related to those aged 16 and over.

title: Disabled in a heatwave: 'We're talking about survival'
description: Disabled campaigners say the official advice for staying safe in a heatwave can put them in more danger.
author: Maddie Molloy
content:
Emily Davison works with a guide dog as she has a visual impairment related to a congenital health condition
Heatwaves this summer have brought travel disruption, overheating homes and school closures for millions - and there is a fifth heatwave expected to hit this week.
It is well-documented that those with existing health conditions and disabilities are most at risk during extreme heat episodes.
But these additional and specific challenges faced - from struggling service dogs to overheating wheelchairs - are often overlooked, even in public advice and emergency planning, say campaigners and researchers.
"For somebody who is able-bodied, it's uncomfortable but if you identify as disabled, we're starting to talk about survival," says campaigner Doug Paulley.
'There's nowhere we can stay': The holiday struggle facing disabled people
NHS must plan for heatwaves like it does for winter, health secretary says
Emily Davison says soaring temperatures force her to put the welfare of her guide dog, Rosie, before her own independence.
"The dog's health has to come first."
Davison is a London-based journalist and content creator, but heatwaves have forced her to cancel journeys to events because it is often too hot for Rosie to travel safely - missing out on potential earnings.
Public transport like buses often overheat and she avoids Uber after "too many experiences where they've not let me in with a dog".
She says finding available taxis has become more difficult, even with London Taxicard scheme, a subsidised taxi service for people with mobility impairments or severe sight loss.
Davison says every trip now requires careful planning, which can make her feel isolated and limits both her work and independence.
"It does put the brakes on your life," she says. "When you're in this situation and you've got a guide dog and you can't do anything, it does make certain things grind to a halt."
She is now spending long periods working from home - but says she is lucky to be still able to do this but not all disabled people can.
"I think the culture of being able to work from home and have that option is really important to keep ensuring that disabled people can still be in employment."
Jimmy Macfarlane uses a wheelchair - when lifts break down in the heat it can leave him stranded
Jimmy Macfarlane is a Cardiff-based actor who needs to travel for his job - so he uses a powered wheelchair.
During this summer's heatwaves, people have taken to social media to report phone batteries draining faster because of the high temperatures, but forJimmy batteries are what enable him to get around.
"The heat definitely impacts the chair and it makes the battery go down a lot quicker.
"I always have to think is there a way I can get to where I need to be without moving the chair?" Macfarlane says.
Some days he has not even been able to leave his home - he previously lived in a sixth-floor flat and the heat caused the lift to break down.
Such problems have been reported in other high-rise buildings by BBC News , but unlike other residents Jimmy cannot just use the stairs to get round the problem.
"There were times where I was stuck in the flat [for days] until it was fixed," he says.
And the heat inside his flat became difficult to manage.
Because of his cerebral palsy, he says everyday tasks already require more energy. "Things like getting changed, having a showerâ?¦ everything I do takes twice as long as a non-disabled person.
"On a hot day, it's even more exhausting."
Common advice for dealing with the heat is to conserve energy and stay cool by keeping your curtains closed and opening the windows when it is cool.
But for Claire Sisk, a content creator and advocate who has distorted vision, this can be dangerous.
"If I've got all my windows and doors open, I feel incredibly vulnerable because I can't see if anybody is walking into my property. So I have to have them all closed, which is quite unbearable," Sisk says.
Claire Sisk gradually lost her sight after suffering two strokes in 2009 when she was aged 29
Other measures intended to keep homes cool can introduce new risks. Fans, for example, can become trip hazards because they are not part of her usual layout.
When she leaves home, the current weather can make her remaining vision far less reliable.
"[When] that sunlight comes out, then that bit of vision just goes," Sisk says.
Hot weather can make travel unpredictable, and access issues can waste valuable time on an already exhausting day. She recalled having to wait at a Tube station because of staff shortages.
"That can be a bit frustrating because it takes you two hours then to get home when it should have only taken 45 minutes."
Hollye Kirkcaldy, a PhD researcher at the University of Bath, studies how extreme heat affects disabled people in the UK, and says these experiences are shared by many across the country.
"You've got inequalities in urban infrastructure, housing, structural conditions around things like social networks and care. If you put all of those together and then you throw heat in, that's what's disabling," Kirkcaldy says.
Her research found that official heatwave guidance often does not reflect disabled people's circumstances, while measures presented as simple can in fact create new barriers.
This can reduce independence which harms their mental wellbeing and adds financial pressures, she says. Disabled people can be left unable to work and facing additional outgoings like higher energy costs for round-the-clock cooling.
Kirkcaldy says in some cases it can be "a trade-off that nobody should have to make between your health and whether you eat."
Doug Paulley campaigns on disability rights and accessibility in public policy
For disability campaigner Doug Paulley, who has a number of health conditions which are exacerbated by hot temperatures, the experiences of disabled people during heatwaves point to wider problems in society.
"Disabled people are always amongst the first against the wall whenever there's a significant crisis of any type in society, and this is no exception," Paulley says.
During one heatwave, he cancelled physiotherapy and missed giving evidence to the Covid Inquiry because travelling became unsafe.
"There was just no way that I could have gone. It was dangerously hot and I would have been really unwell."
Climate change must be factored into how people think about access and support, Emily Davison says.
"Climate change is a thing. Summers are only going to get hotter."
For Doug, the issue is not only how disabled people cope with extreme weather, but whose experiences are considered when decisions are made about the future.
"Policy is very much set for them, not with them."

title: BBC seeks to subpoena Trump's family members in Panorama lawsuit
description: A spokesperson for Trump's legal team responded to the request accusing the broadcaster of "seeking to harass" the president's family.
author: Tom Bateman
content:
The BBC has sought to subpoena members of Donald Trump's family for documents and testimony in the US president's $10bn (Â£7.4bn) defamation lawsuit against the broadcaster.
Court filings show that representatives for the BBC's legal team attempted in May to serve subpoenas to the president's son Donald Trump Jr, his daughter Ivanka Trump and son-in-law Jared Kushner.
The president is suing the BBC over an episode of Panorama that edited together two different sections of a speech he gave before the 2021 Capitol riots.
The BBC has previously apologised for the edit, but denied it was grounds for defamation.
Judge grants Trump's request to delay handing financial records to BBC
In a statement to the BBC, a spokesman for Trump's legal team said the BBC had "intentionally defamed" the president, and with its subpoena request was now "seeking to harass him, his family, and supporters by abusing the deposition process".
"The BBC is simply trying to distract away from their own obvious liability," the statement said.
The BBC's lawyers argue in the latest filing that Trump's family members had "personal knowledge" of his intentions in delivering the speech, making their testimony and documents relevant to the president's defamation claim.
Drawing on evidence previously gathered by a US congressional committee, the filing says Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present when their father revised and delivered his speech, adding that Jared Kushner drafted a proposed statement for him that would have condemned the use of violence.
The filing asks the court to allow the subpoenas to be served by email and certified mail, saying attempts to serve them by hand were unsuccessful.
A subpoena is an order for someone to answer questions under oath or provide evidence. Failure to comply results in a penalty.
According to court filings, in one instance, a representative for the BBC's legal team tried to deliver a subpoena for Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner at their home in Florida, but was refused entry at a police checkpoint and was later told by the Secret Service that the agency could not accept the subpoenas.
Similarly, according to the filing, a representative tried to serve a subpoena for Donald Trump Jr at Trump Tower in New York but was told by the concierge that the person who normally took such documents may have been at lunch.
During another attempt two days later, the representative was told the "legal department" was not in that day, according to the filing.
The BBC press office declined to comment.
Trump drops BBC's commercial arm from Panorama lawsuit, but main case remains
Last December, Trump sued the BBC and subsidiaries BBC Studios Productions and BBC Studios Distribution over the 2024 Panorama episode.
Trump's lawsuit - filed in Florida - accuses the BBC of "intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring" the speech he gave outside the Capitol on 6 January 2021.
The BBC has apologised for an editing error that gave "the mistaken impression that President Trump had made a direct call for violent action".
However, the BBC has asked the court to dismiss the lawsuit, arguing that the programme did not meet the legal criteria for defamation and was not made available on its US platforms.
Last month, Trump's lawyers admitted they had no evidence that the documentary was available in the US on the BBC's BritBox subscription service, as they had originally claimed, or on BBC.com, BBC Select or through US broadcasters.
Trump also recently agreed to drop the BBC's commercial arm BBC Studios from his lawsuit, after the BBC argued the company had "no role in creating or producing the documentary".
Earlier this month, the judge in the case granted Trump's request for a delay in him handing over financial documents to the broadcaster as part of the lawsuit.
The BBC has asked for some of Trump's financial records in relation to his argument that the documentary damaged the president's business interests.
The president's legal team said disclosure of the financial records would cause him "irreparable harm".
A trial date in February 2027 has been scheduled, should the case progress.
BBC News is editorially independent from the wider corporation.

title: Harvey Nichols bought by owner of Sports Direct
description: The department store made famous by sitcom Absolutely Fabulous had warned it would cease trading.
author: Yasmin Rufo
content:
Luxury department store Harvey Nichols has been bought by the owner of Sports Direct, which warned a "significant restructuring" was needed to ensure the 200-year-old business remains sustainable.
Mike Ashley's Frasers Group will take control of the Harvey Nichols stores, including its flagship in Knightsbridge, as well as the international franchise.
The department store was immortalised in BBC sitcom Absolutely Fabulous, but had faced challenges in recent years. The firm had appointed administrators in June.
Michael Murray, Frasers' chief executive and Ashley's son-in-law, called the store a "British institution with significant potential" but added "clear meaningful change is needed".
"The turnaround will require tough choices and we are prepared to make those decisions, even if that means a smaller business in the near term, to create a stronger and more sustainable Harvey Nichols for the long-term," he said.
Harvey Nichols carries more than 800 premium and luxury brands and has over 1,000 employees. Its other stores are located in Manchester, Birmingham, Bristol, Leeds and Edinburgh.
Frasers Group will also acquire the online business, and shops will continue to operate under their existing licensing.
Earlier this week, Harvey Nichols warned in its latest accounts that it would need to "cease trading" within a year if it failed to secure new investment.
It had faced "sustained trading and operational challenges" recently and Frasers Group said it will need to conduct a review of the store's portfolio, structure and cost base.
A recent auction for the store saw Frasers battle retail rival Next to take control of the firm.
Harvey Nichols was bought in 1991 by Hong Kong-based businessman Sir Dickson Poon but he put the group up for sale earlier this year.
Edina and Patsy from Absolutely Fabulous made frequent retail therapy trips to "Harvey Nicks"
Dubbed "Harvey Nicks" by Edina and Patsy from Absolutely Fabulous, the two often found an excuse to nip into the department store for a spot of shopping and a long liquid lunch in the heyday of the 1990s.
But Catherine Shuttleworth, retail expert and boss of Savvy Marketing, said: "If you go into a Harvey Nicks store - and I did last week - they look terrible, they look really tired and basically they've suffered from a lack of investment."
She told BBC Wake Up to Money that department stores "are cash-hungry monsters, they need investing, they need to look good and if you're at the top of the luxury market that's got to be constant".
Harvey Nichols chief executive Julia Goddard said the deal marked "an important milestone" for the company and "provides a strong platform for the next phase of the business's evolution".
"Over the past year, we have made significant progress in repositioning this iconic business, investing in our flagship store, broadening our customer proposition, and strengthening the brand DNA," she added.
As well as Sports Direct, Frasers has bought up a huge number of retailers and their brands over the years. These include upmarket fashion chain Flannels, Savile Row tailor Gieves & Hawkes and luxury lingerie firm Agent Provocateur.
It also owns Jack Wills and House of Fraser.
Shuttleworth said Frasers' boss Murray has "got his finger right on the pulse of how those [young] shoppers shop".
"If you look at what the group have done with Flannels, [Harvey Nichols] is going to be more Flannel-esque than it is going to be Sports Direct-esque," she said.
Fraser Group's purchase of Harvey Nichols is part of its strategy to increase its presence in the luxury section.
It recently launched a takeover approach for German brand Hugo Boss, which it has a stake in already.
Lindsay Hallam, senior managing director of administrator FTI Consulting, who advised Frasers Group on the sale, said she was "pleased to have secured a buyer, providing continuity for Harvey Nichols and enabling it to move forward under new ownership".
"We are particularly pleased the transaction secures more than 1,000 jobs and provides a strong platform for its next chapter.
"Our focus was to find a solution that protected the underlying value of the business, securing a future for a 200-year-old retailer, and delivering the best possible outcome for stakeholders".
Harvey Nichols's restaurant in the Oxo Tower, London is being sold off separately and is not included in the deal.

title: The serial candidates standing against Farage in Clacton
description: BBC Verify takes a look at the serial candidates standing in Clacton, how they fared in previous elections, and whether they have ever won enough votes to get their deposits back.
author: Rob England, Jess Carr
content:
A record number of candidates are standing in next week's Clacton by-election, but some names on the ballot will be more familiar than others.
As the main parties are not standing against Reform UK leader Nigel Farage, the 33 other candidates on the ballot are either from smaller political parties or are standing as independents.
Nine of these names have already appeared on multiple ballot papers elsewhere in the UK, including Reclaim Party leader Laurence Fox and satirical candidates Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope.
BBC Verify has taken a look at the serial candidates who have decided to stand in Clacton, how they have fared in previous elections, and whether they have ever won enough votes to save their Â£500 parliamentary - or Â£10,000 London mayor - deposits.
The Clacton by-election takes place on 13 August, and because there are a total of 34 people contesting the seat it means people in the constituency will be casting their votes on what is understood to be the longest ballot paper in British electoral history.
Using confirmed parliamentary records, we found nine candidates standing against Farage who have stood at least twice before in Westminster parliamentary or London mayoral elections.
They are: Rejoin EU candidate John Stevens, Social Democratic Party leader William Clouston, Reclaim leader Laurence Fox, independent Joseph 77, Count Binface, independent Andy Erlam, and three candidates from the Monster Raving Loony Party - leader Howling Laud Hope, Nick the Incredible Flying Brick and Baron Von Thunderclap.
The Clacton by-election ballot paper
UK electoral law does not prevent a registered political party from fielding more than one candidate in a parliamentary by-election. Each candidate must have a valid nomination and be authorised by the party's nominating officer.
Nigel Farage has previously stood in seven parliamentary contests since 1994, and successfully became an MP for Clacton in the 2024 general election.
Parliamentary candidates do not have to be from the area they want to stand in to appear on the ballot, but they do have to be nominated by 10 people who live in the constituency.
A Â£500 deposit is also required to validate their candidacy, which they only get back if they achieve more than 5% of the vote share.
Mayoral elections have stricter eligibility rules. For example, in London candidates must either live, work or be registered to vote in the capital, or rent or own a property in the city. They must also get at least 10 nominations from each London borough and at least 10 from the City of London, and win more than 5% of the vote share to have their Â£10,000 deposit returned.
Howling Laud Hope, the leader of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party, has previously stood in 37 parliamentary elections since 1983.
Real name Alan Hope, the party leader challenged David Cameron's seat when he was elected prime minister in 2010, and stood against former prime minister Theresa May in the 2017 general election.
He gained his highest share of the vote in the 2011 Leicester South by-election, which was held by Labour. Hope finished last of five candidates, with 553 votes, or 1.6%.
He has never won enough votes to get back a Â£500 parliamentary deposit.
Previous attempts: 37
Nick the Incredible Flying Brick, whose real name is Nick Delves, has previously stood for the Official Monster Raving Loony Party in 13 parliamentary contests.
He stood against former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer in the 2024 general election, but his highest share of the vote came in West Derbyshire at the 2001 general election, when the Conservatives held the seat. He finished fifth of six candidates with 472 votes, or 0.9% of all votes.
Like Hope, he has never won enough votes to get back a Â£500 parliamentary deposit.
Previous attempts: 13
Tom Darwood, who stands under the name Joseph 77, has previously contested eight parliamentary elections.
The strongest of those runs came in Southend West in Essex at the 2019 general election. He received 574 votes, or 1.2%, in a seat held by the Conservatives.
Darwood has never won enough votes to get back a Â£500 parliamentary deposit.
Count Binface is the satirical alter ego of comedian Jon Harvey, who has previously stood in four parliamentary elections and two London mayoral elections.
As Count Binface, Harvey has been on the same ballot as two sitting prime ministers during a general election - Boris Johnson in 2019 and Rishi Sunak in 2024 - and separately stood as a different character, Lord Buckethead, against Theresa May in Maidenhead in 2017.
In 2023 Count Binface stood in the Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election after Johnson resigned as an MP, and in June this year he stood against now prime minister Andy Burnham in the Makerfield by-election.
His best parliamentary result came in the Richmond and Northallerton vote against Sunak in the 2024 general election. He gained 308 votes - 0.6% of the total share - and finished sixth out of 13 candidates.
He has not previously won enough votes to get back any of his deposits.
Baron Von Thunderclap - real name Peter Berry - is the third Official Monster Raving Loony Party candidate on the ballot. He previously stood in six parliamentary elections.
The Clacton contest is his first parliamentary by-election however, and his first parliamentary race outside Mid Sussex. His strongest turnout was during the 2001 general election, when he received 601 votes, or 1.3% of the vote share. He finished fifth out of five candidates and the Conservatives held the seat.
Former Conservative MEP John Stevens, who is standing for the Rejoin EU Party, has previously appeared on the ballot in four parliamentary elections.
His best result came as an independent in Buckingham in the 2010 general election, when he challenged then speaker of the House of Commons John Bercow. The main parties do not usually stand against the Speaker in a general election, and Stevens finished second of 11 candidates with 10,331 votes, a 21.4% vote share. Farage also challenged Bercow for the seat that year and came third.
It means Stevens is the only Clacton candidate to have stood against and won more votes than Farage in a parliamentary contest. Stevens also gained enough votes to qualify to have his deposit returned.
William Clouston, the leader of the Social Democratic Party, previously stood in three parliamentary elections.
His best result came in Durham North West, in the 2001 general election, when Labour held the seat. Clouston, standing as a Conservative, finished second of four candidates with 8,193 votes, or 20.9% of the vote share.
This was enough votes to retain his Â£500 parliamentary deposit.
Andy Erlam has previously contested three parliamentary elections.
His best run was in Bexleyheath in London at the 1983 general election. He received 7,560 votes, or 17.1%, in a seat held by the Conservatives.
Erlam won enough votes to get back two of his parliamentary deposits.
Actor turned right-wing commentator Laurence Fox, of the Reclaim Party, has previously stood in one parliamentary by-election and one London mayoral election.
His only parliamentary contest before Clacton was the 2023 Uxbridge and South Ruislip by-election. Fox finished fourth out of 17 candidates. The Conservatives held the seat, while Fox received 714 votes, or a 2.3% share of the vote.
He did not win enough votes to get back either of his deposits.
For this analysis, the BBC counted previous UK House of Commons elections dating back to 1955, by-elections to 1983 and Mayor of London records to 2000. Results prior to this are not included in the analysis.
The current Clacton contest counts towards the three-contest threshold to be included in the analysis.
Local council elections, local and combined-authority mayoral elections, devolved legislatures, European Parliament elections and London Assembly elections were excluded.
Official records do not track individual candidates over time and there can be discrepancies where individuals are recorded under different variations on their name, aliases, or for different parties across their careers.
Correction 6 August 2026: This article has been amended to include details found through historical data where candidate names and political parties were recorded inconsistently. We have updated the text and graphics relating to William Clouston and Joseph 77 to add one more election each to their totals, and added an additional candidate to our analysis, Andy Erlam, who met the threshold for inclusion.

title: Peterborough residents urged to avoid fireworks in heat spell
description: MPs say crews are under pressure due to wildfires, including the large one at a nature reserve.
author: Shariqua Ahmed
content:
Labour MPs Andrew Pakes and Sam Carling, alongside council leader Shabina Qayyum, are urging people not to let off fireworks
Two MPs and the council leader have urged people to stop setting off "nuisance" fireworks during the heatwave to stop fires taking hold.
In an open letter, Peterborough's Labour MPs Andrew Pakes and Sam Carling, and Labour city council leader Shabina Qayyum asked people to "think twice" due to the "tinder-dry conditions".
They also cited "ongoing noise nuisance caused by anti-social, late-night firework use in recent days" and also advised people against using disposable barbecues.
Pakes said: "Fireworks can be brilliant fun when they're organised and done properly, but right now, in this heat, with everything as dry as it is, a single spark is all it takes to cause real damage."
Tinderbox conditions have been cited as exacerbating the wildfire at Holme Fen Nature Reserve near Ramsey
He added that firefighters were already under significant pressure and said residents could help reduce the risk by avoiding activities that could ignite dry vegetation.
The letter references Cambridgeshire Fire and Rescue Service's continued efforts to tackle a major peatland fire at Holme Fen Nature Reserve, which has occupied crews since Saturday . The cause of the fire is yet to be established.
The BBC has asked the fire service how many firework-related incidents they have attended in recent weeks.
Carling, MP for the North West Cambridgeshire constituency, which includes Holme Fen, said: "This isn't about spoiling anyone's fun; it's about recognising that conditions right now make fireworks and disposable barbecues genuinely dangerous."
Qayyum added: "I'd urge everyone to exercise real caution. That means thinking twice about fireworks and disposable barbecues, and looking out for each other by speaking up if you see something risky."
The Nene Park Trust has banned the use of disposable barbecues in its parks, including at Ferry Meadows in Peterborough.
The fire service is urging residents to use fireworks responsibly, including supervising sparklers carefully, and reminding people that fireworks must not be sold to under-18s or set off in public places.
Cambridgeshire Police said it had received one report in the past week relating to fireworks being let off near homes.
The call was made by a concerned resident in Dogsthorpe in Peterborough at about 22:00 BST on Monday.
On Wednesday, residents of the Longthorpe and Netherton area of the city said fireworks were being let off for periods of several minutes during the daytime.

title: Are the UK's top universities really 'hoovering up' students?
description: The most selective universities have seen the biggest rise in students accepted onto their courses for 2026.
author: Beth Rose
content:
A record number of UK 18-year-olds have been accepted into university this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas).
But the biggest increase in acceptances was for the most selective, "higher-tariff" universities â?? such as those in the Russell Group.
Nick Hillman, chief executive of the Higher Education Policy Institute (Hepi), said the top institutions were "hoovering up all the crumbs" when it came to the top students, even if they had not met the grades they had been offered.
The Russell Group itself said there was "always some flexibility in admissions decisions", and that this "should not be confused with lowering standards".
The Department for Education (DfE) said while universities were independent of government, it was "essential that standards are maintained and that the students they admit are likely to succeed".
The number of students accepted into higher-tariff universities in 2026 was 5.5% higher than last year.
By comparison, for medium-tariff universities - where students tend to get in with fewer Ucas points than the more selective universities - acceptances increased by 3.8%.
And acceptances at lower-tariff universities fell by 1.7% year-on-year.
The increase at the more selective universities comes at a time when the sector has been struggling financially as a whole, and questions have been raised about the importance of degrees and the cost of going to university.
"Universities are like every other institution, they want to be bigger and better next year," said Nick Hillman, chief executive of Hepi.
"If you can recruit good students, why wouldn't you?"
He said universities taking on more students meant less popular courses, such as modern languages, could be kept running, keeping staff redundancies at bay.
While there had been a "significant drop in international students" - who are largely postgraduates, and who pay higher fees - Hillman said universities were utilising their resources for UK undergraduates instead.
As it congratulated the 2026 cohort of new students, the Russell Group was quick to dampen down any questions that a boost in student numbers was a result of "lowering standards", and said it would "remain highly selective"
It said: "While there is always some flexibility in admissions decisions, this should not be confused with lowering standards. Our universities will only admit students who show evidence of being able to succeed on the course."
Five key takeaways from results day 2026
Everything you need to know about university costs
'I worked really hard and it paid off': Elation, nerves and proud parents as students get results
Duncan Ivison, president and vice chancellor at The University of Manchester, said students had been working hard to get the places they wanted and deserved.
"We're not cutting our standards," he said.
"We want our students not just to pass, but really flourish and do well. You can't admit students who aren't going to be able to take advantage of the opportunity that universities are offering."
The university said that, for the first time, it had received more than 100,000 applications this year â?? an increase of 13%.
A further 8,000 conversations were expected to take place through Clearing on results day alone.
For A-level student Stephen, from Carmel College in St Helens, results day turned into a "miraculous" morning after New College, Oxford, accepted him to study law despite him missing the grades he had been offered.
"When I opened my slip, I was initially really disappointed. I'd been made an offer of three As. I came out with ABB," he said.
"Then it was miraculous, I opened my Ucas form and I'd had my place confirmed.
"I'm absolutely over the moon."
Stephen initially thought he'd missed his chance of a place at Oxford
It was a big relief for Niamh, too, who studies at the same college in the North West.
She told the BBC she had her heart set on studying midwifery at Edge Hill University in Ormskirk, Lancashire, but was turned down at the application stage and told she did not have the grades.
She had planned to go through Clearing and try her luck again, but was instead offered a place by the university about a month ago.
She said she was "really happy" and wanted to "empower women" and "leave an imprint on their lives" with her future career.
Niamh is off to study midwifery after her application was initially turned down
Universities UK, which represents 142 institutions, said the changes in student acceptance numbers was not necessarily as simple as the top universities grabbing as many students as they could by lowering grades.
Chief executive Vivienne Stern said the grade profiles accepted by different universities were "more or less identical to the pattern in previous years".
There are numerous reasons why students might be offered places with higher or lower grade requirements than average, she said, such as certain courses being under-subscribed.
While the financial situation of the higher education sector may have brought the issue to the fore, she said there were "checks and balances" in place.
"The important thing is we've got a system which regulates universities on outcomes," she said.
"You can recruit a student, but we're going to hold you to account. It's not in the interest to recruit a student who is not well equipped to succeed."
Hillman, from Hepi, said while universities were likely to be "breathing a sigh of relief" over the high student numbers, the true picture would only become clear once the new term begins.
A DfE spokesperson said ministers were "taking action to restore universities as engines of opportunity, aspiration and growth" and making sure they had a secure future.
"We are putting them on a firmer financial footing, including by raising tuition fee caps in line with forecast inflation and the Office for Students refocusing on monitoring the financial health of the sector."

title: Antarctica's first ever dinosaur bone discovered in a drawer
description: The fossil, collected in Antarctica in 1985, is part of the tail of a beast called a Titanosaur.
author: Rebecca Morelle , Alison Francis
content:
The fossil was originally found in 1985 on James Ross Island in Antarctica
An unassuming-looking fossil that spent 40 years lying forgotten in a drawer has turned out to be the first dinosaur bone ever found in Antarctica.
The specimen was unearthed in 1985, but the team that discovered it was not sure what it was - so it was stored away in the geology collection of the British Antarctic Survey (BAS) in Cambridge.
Now the fossil has been studied by palaeontologists who have confirmed that it is a tail bone from a type of dinosaur called a Titanosaur - this group contained the largest dinosaurs to ever walk the Earth.
The discovery helps to reveal more about how these beasts lived in a part of the world where the fossil record is sparse.
The discovery was recorded in geologist Mike Thomson's notebook
Dr Mark Evans, the collections manager at BAS, recently spotted the fossil amongst thousands of specimens brought back from expeditions to Antarctica over the decades.
"It's only when you start thinking 'what's in this drawer', that sometimes you come across something and you think, 'Ah, this looks interesting'," he said.
The specimen was originally collected on James Ross Island and its discovery was recorded in a field notebook kept by geologist Dr Mike Thomson.
Alongside a tiny, neat sketch of the fossil dated 9 December 1985 he has written "vertebra of large reptile", noting it was about 10cm wide.
Evans says the team that found it probably thought the fossil belonged to a marine reptile.
But as soon as he saw it, Evans realised the vertebra looked very dinosaur-like. And the date of its discovery meant it would have been the first dinosaur fossil found on the continent.
When Titanosaurs inhabited Antarctica 80 million years ago it would have been covered in lush forest
He called in Prof Paul Barrett from the Natural History Museum (NHM) to confirm his discovery.
"Although it's not too much to look at, it actually has a really distinctive shape," Barrett told us, holding the fossil in his hands.
He pointed to a hollow on one end of the fossil and then turned it over to reveal a rounded bump at the other. The vertebrae line up to create a series of ball-and-socket joints running from head to tail.
"As soon as I saw it, I knew what we were dealing withâ?¦ it was a dead cert we were dealing with a Titanosaur," he said. "This is a combination of features that's completely unique to these types of dinosaurs."
A Titanosaur cast, on loan from the NHM, is on display at Peterborough Cathedral
More than 100 species of Titanosaur have now been identified around the world.
All are four-legged plant eaters, with very long necks that helped them reach up into trees and long counter-balancing tails. The very biggest Titanosaurs were more than 115ft (35m) long and weighed about 60 tonnes.
From the size of this tail bone, the scientists estimate the Antarctic Titanosaur was about 23ft (7m) in length.
"Maybe it was a juvenile dinosaur, or maybe it was a genuinely small one - one that was actually bucking the trend for the rest of the group as a smaller adult," explained Barrett.
This dinosaur would have lived 82 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous Period when Antarctica was very different from how it is today. It would have been covered in lush forest, providing ample food for the plant-eating beast.
Dr Mark Evans spotted the fossil in the British Antarctic Survey's geology collections
The long-forgotten fossil now holds an important place in the history of exploration in Antarctica. Other dinosaur fossils have been found in this remote part of the world in the years after 1985 - but not very many.
Antarctica is a challenging place for palaeontologists to work and the ice conceals the prehistoric record in the rock beneath.
"It shows that an area that we now think is really uninhabitable was once actually very habitable and had this huge cast of characters living on it," explained Barrett.
"It's helping us to work out how they fitted into these broader ecosystems at the very bottom of the world about 80 million years ago."
AÂ paper on the discovery , external has been published in the journal Acta Palaeontologica Polonica.

title: Prisoner release row proving to be Burnham's first big test as PM
description: The prison overcrowding crisis presents the new PM with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices.
author: Damian Grammaticas
content:
Three weeks into his premiership, Andy Burnham has "hit bumps in the road" in the estimation of one long-serving Labour MP with the row over the early release of some prisoners from jail.
His political opponents are already sharpening their attacks, believing they have found an issue with which to discomfit a new prime minister early in his time in office who had, until now, displayed a pretty deft political touch.
Conservative Shadow Home Secretary Chris Philp said: "This the most important decision Andy Burnham has made since he became prime minister and he's got it wrong."
For Labour MPs, however, this week has shown Burnham is prepared to confront difficult choices and take decisions which, as he said in his first speech in Downing Street, are "more about problem solving than point scoring".
Burnham's first two weeks in the job were pretty problem free, with a succession of announcements, from a cap on bus fares to a determination to overhaul of social care, along with a blitz of social media videos, all designed to portray a more relaxed PM with a focus on everyday issues.
The overcrowding crisis in our prisons has presented him with a dilemma for which there are only unpalatable choices.
Crucially too, they are some of the first difficult choices Burnham has had to make in office.
The issue long predates his arrival in Downing Street. In 2023, with space in jails on the verge of running out, the last Conservative government started releasing prisoners 18 days early. That was only a temporary fix.
Just days after becoming prime minister in July 2024, Sir Keir Starmer had to contemplate a more far-reaching prisoner release scheme, saying "it is shocking for our country to have got into a state where we have too many prisoners and not enough prison places".
In January this year, Sir Keir's government passed the Sentencing Act under which several thousand prisoners will be released early starting this autumn, including some convicted of very serious crimes.
HMP Wandsworth, in London, is Britain's most overcrowded prison
Andy Burnham, aware of how sensitive this would be, immediately ordered a review.
His frustration was evident when he announced he was removing some categories of prisoner from early release, rapists and child sex offenders among them, but not others.
"The truth is I wanted to go even further," he said, "I have pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".
The Conservatives seized on the fact that his decisions mean that among those still being let out early will be some who committed grooming-related crimes as well as some killers, including those of PC Andrew Harper.
"The Labour government has made mistake after mistake on this early release scheme," said Chris Philp.
"Despite our warnings in Parliament, they initially planned to release rapists and dangerous criminals.
"But, even after Andy Burnham's review, it turns out they still plan to release cop-killers and men involved in the grooming gang scandal early. It's an insult to PC Harper's family and many other victims."
Up against Sir Keir, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch managed to find issues she could use to force him on to the back foot and into what turned out to be a damaging series of policy shifts. She has seized on the early releases to do try to do the same with his successor.
A first sign of that came when Burnham had to "personally intervene" this week, his spokesperson said, to order officials to find out how many people convicted of grooming-related offences might still be getting early release.
That came after Badenoch highlighted the issue in an open letter to him.
The Conservatives are now considering how they can keep the pressure up when parliament returns in September.
They will aim to place Labour MPs in an uncomfortable position if the issue can be debated in the Commons.
What's behind having to release some prisoners early?
Officer who led PC Harper investigation 'appalled' killers could be released early
Burnham orders review of grooming gang early releases
Justice secretary apologises to families affected by early release scheme
Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy has called on the government to introduce "emergency primary legislation as soon as Parliament returns in September," as he says that is the only way to permanently exclude "killers - like the killers of PC Harper - child abusers and grooming gang members from early release".
For now, Labour MPs are off on their summer breaks.
"There is no point in bemoaning what is going on" one says phlegmatically, "Andy Burnham's inherited this vexed issue that our jails are full, it's in the nature of being PM.".
"I have every confidence in him. Over all the years Andy Burnham has never been fearful of speaking to victims directly," adds the MP who has served on the justice select committee.
But they added: "We need to have an honest conversation about who we are sending to jail as we don't have the spaces to accommodate everyone we are sending."
Another MP, from the left of the party, said Labour members still felt overwhelmingly positive about their new leader despite the row over prisoner releases.
"They don't believe he has a magic wand. I don't blame him for the overcrowding crisis and I don't think voters do".
And the MP added "at least we have a recognisably Labour government. It feels like we are in play again, with a second chance to make a difference, maybe even to win a second term".

title: Cattle cull: Muir says days of the UFU 'dictating government policy are over'
description: The Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir says he will continue to engage with the Ulster Farmers' Union.
author: Louise Cullen, Finn Purdy
content:
There have been calls for the Agriculture Minister, Andrew Muir, to resign
The Agriculture Minister Andrew Muir has said "the days of the Ulster Farmers' Union (UFU) dictating government policy are over".
It comes after the UFU extended a vote of no confidence in the department to include the minister, the permanent secretary and the chief vet, over how a cull of 51 cattle was carried out in County Tyrone.
The cows were shot in June, leading to complaints about the manner of the cull which was carried out within earshot of members of the public.
The UFU President John McLenaghan had said there were concerns about the independence of a Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) review into the incident.
Muir said he would continue to engage with the UFU and had spoken with its president on Friday morning.
He added that the situation he had inherited in the department was "extremely challenging", with issues building up "due to wrong government policy previously".
He said he was "arguably the first minister in the history of this state that is not beholden to one vested interest".
Muir described some of the speeches at a protest outside Stormont on Monday as "pure electioneering" and called on his fellow politicians to "calm it down".
Earlier this week, Muir said a death threat had been made against him . He also received one in June .
On Friday, he said "the police will be coming looking" for those who threatened or abused anyone in public life.
In a statement to BBC News NI, the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) said it does "not discuss the security of individuals and no inference should be drawn from this".
"However, we will continue to do all we can to ensure that all of our politicians are supported and that they can undertake their role free from fear and intimidation," Insp Roberts said.
The UFU also called for Daera's Permanent Secretary Katrina Godfrey and the Chief Veterinary Officer Brian Dooher to resign.
In response, the senior civil servants' union the FDA said it was "entirely inappropriate" to call for the resignation of officials who were "duty-bound to serve ministers" and "could not defend themselves publicly".
The minister has previously said there was no reasonable alternative to the cattle being euthanised on site and has insisted it was a last resort as officials had to act on a court order.
An external review of the cattle cull was announced by Daera earlier this month , but the UFU's Executive Committee met on Thursday night.
Ulster Farmers' Union president John McLenaghan said the UFU "no longer have confidence that the Department can deliver"
In a statement on Friday the UFU said it "does not have the confidence in the independence of the review as presently constituted, including the scope of the Terms of Reference and appointment of a single person to conduct it.
"The UFU has consistently maintained that an investigation into an incident of this seriousness must be demonstrably independent, robust and capable of commanding the confidence of farm families and the wider public."
John McLenaghan said calling for resignations was not a decision his union had taken "lightly".
However he added that confidence had been "severely damaged".
He said the most recent event is "just one of many instances where farmers feel that the Department has lost touch with farmers".
"We no longer have confidence that the department can deliver."
A Daera spokesperson said they and the minister were aware of the decision.
"An external independent review is already underway to review the action taken by Department officials in response to the Deprivation Order in Fivemiletown," they continued.
"There are many strategic issues and challenges for agriculture.
"It is vital we face up to those challenges together to restore our environment and ensure a sustainable future for agriculture".
Responding to the vote against the two named senior officials, the FDA union's Robert Murtagh said: "This kind of performative stunt, naming and targeting officials, does not aid understanding and undermines the need for constructive dialogue.
"The UFU's action appears also to be seeking to pre-empt and to influence the independent review already now in train.
"It should be awaiting its findings and recommendations before jumping to respond to voices who do not care about public service or indeed public servants."
Warning: This article contains an image of dead animals that some may find distressing
Animal welfare inspections on the farm dating back to 2022 identified serious concerns, including 33 animal carcasses, feed contaminated with urine and faeces, and emaciated animals.
The farmer was found guilty of a number of animal welfare offences in May and disqualified from keeping animals for life.
The offences included:
Thirteen charges of failure to dispose of an animal carcass
One charge of failure to comply with an Animal By-Products notice
Six charges of causing unnecessary suffering to an animal
One charge of failure to produce medicine records
The court issued a deprivation order on 8 June - that the farmer must have the animals removed from his ownership.
As is practice, he was given two weeks to appeal the sentence, or to transfer, sell or give away his stock.
He was then given an extra week.
On 29 June, when the extended grace period had lapsed, the departmental humane slaughter team arrived at the farm to begin destruction of the remaining 51 animals by shooting them.
The operation was completed on 30 June.
Some members of the public witnessed the operation in one of the three areas across the farm that the animals were in.
Questions about how the operation was conducted were first raised by a local councillor, then concerns were expressed by politicians and farming leaders.
The AERA committee was recalled to discuss the incident, and quiz the minister and veterinary officials.
The committee heard that officials had been working with the farmer after "numerous" inspections, beginning in 2022.
The agriculture minister Andrew Muir said those had revealed a "grotesque" situation and "a large number of animals were caused unnecessary suffering", leading to the deprivation order.
"That order legally required the department to deprive the individual of any livestock.
"The department had no choice.
"And so my officials took the necessary steps to fulfil this legal obligation."
It emerged that a total of 21 animals had been removed during the grace period, but 51 remained on the farm.
The cattle were shot dead in a field in County Tyrone in June
Officials said animals in two of the areas on the farm were disposed of by 13:30 on 29 June.
The slaughter operation in the final area was stopped when a local farmer offered to buy some of the remaining cattle.
But the animals could not be rounded up, and escaped onto the road.
They were eventually herded back and a vet recommended they be shot.
One remaining animal was disposed of on 30 June.
The carcasses were removed later that day.
Questions have been asked about the weapons used, the amount of ammunition, and why slaughter in situ was chosen as the method of disposal.
Deputy Chief Veterinary Officer Gemma Daly described the cattle as "semi-feral" and said staff had expressed concerns over the years about how to handle the animals without causing them stress, or risking injury to themselves.
Senior Principal Veterinary Officer Elsie McGarvey said the department was "technically" potentially in breach of the court order by extending the grace period.
She added that approximately half of the animals were not suitable for the food chain and others were too young.
And she said officials were "always prepared" that the farmer would be disqualified and they "knew" removing the animals would present "significant issues".
Before the committee met, the minister announced that an independent external review , external would be conducted.
It will be led by Dr Martin Blake, a former Chief Veterinary Officer for Ireland.
His work will include looking at the decision-making, risk assessments and communication around the operation.
He will make recommendations, based on his examination of the records and any interviews he carries out.
Muir said Dr Blake's review would be "thorough but not prolonged", and told the committee it would be complete "by early autumn".
The UFU has called for the review to be conducted by a panel of experts, rather than an individual.
Agriculture and environment are uncomfortable but inseparable bedfellows under the department.
And the relationship between Daera and the UFU has been fractious in the past.
The UFU's Executive passed a vote of no confidence in the department - not the minister - in October last year.
That came after an outcry over the initial consultation document for the Nutrients Action Programme.
It has since been revised by a stakeholder group of farmers, agri-food representatives, conservationists and environmental groups.
But the size of the protest on Monday about this incident shows farmers are not happy.
The findings of Dr Blake's review will be closely scrutinised.
The Democratic Unionist Party (DUP) has tabled a motion of no confidence in Andrew Muir which requires 30 signatures to make it to the floor of the Assembly.
But any change at the top of the department would have to come from the minister's party - or the minister himself.
And there are just seven months left for this minister to get a substantial number of significant policies past the Executive.
A deprivation order may be issued by a court when a person is convicted of animal welfare charges.
It requires that person to be deprived of ownership of the animal - to have it taken away - and for the animal to be disposed of.
The court may specify how that disposal will happen, or it may delegate that decision to a person appointed to carry out the order.
The legislation , external states that "disposal" includes destroying an animal.

title: What are BTecs and how are they graded?
description: Hundreds of thousands of students do the vocational qualifications known as BTecs every year.
author: BBC News
content:
As GCSE students prepare to receive their exam results, many will be considering their options for further study, including vocational qualifications such as BTecs.
But what are BTecs, and how are they marked? Here is everything you need to know.
A BTec, which stands for the Business and Technology Education Council, is a practical qualification available in England, Wales and Northern Ireland.
Scotland has its own vocational courses managed by the Scottish Qualifications Authority.
BTec courses are assessed through exams, regular coursework and projects, and sometimes placements.
BTec Firsts are Level 2 qualifications, meaning they are equivalent to GCSEs. Students often take a mixture of the two. They can be helpful for people trying to get into further education colleges.
BTec Nationals are Level 3 qualifications, so can be taken alongside or instead of A-levels.
They are studied over one or two years.
Research suggests one in four students use them as a route into university, while others gain occupation-specific skills and go straight into employment.
BTecs are graded on a scale:
Starred Distinction/Distinction Star (D*)
Some BTecs are worth two or three A-levels.
Students normally receive their results on the same days as A-level and GCSE students, but some receive them before this.
Hundreds of thousands of students study BTEC qualifications and other vocational courses across the UK.
Popular subjects include health and social care, applied science, construction, engineering, business and art and design.
BTec Nationals can be sat by any age group. In fact, most are taken by those over the age of 22 , external as they develop practical career skills.
They are particularly popular among white working class students, according to research by the Social Market Foundation think tank , external .
Other vocational courses are available in the UK, including National Vocational Qualifications , external (NVQs), TechBacs , external , Cambridge Technicals , external and Scottish Vocational Qualifications , external (SVQs).
BTec results normally come out on the same days as A-level and GCSE results
BTecs are part of wider changes to post-16 education in England.
The government has been reviewing vocational qualifications to simplify the system and ensure courses provide the skills needed by students and employers.
Some qualifications that overlap with newer technical qualifications, such as T-levels, have had funding withdrawn, while others have been retained.
BTecs will be defunded to make way for new V-Levels , which will be introduced in stages from September 2027.
T-levels are also continuing to expand as part of reforms to technical education, although the new qualifications have faced challenges including delays, concerns over student retention and issues with some assessments.
