title: Who is new chancellor John Healey? Labour veteran who quit as defence secretary
description: The former defence secretary is seen as a safe pair of hands - and is now in charge of the government's finances.
author: Brian Wheeler
content:
John Healey - who has been announced as Andy Burnham's Chancellor of the Exchequer - is seen as the ultimate safe pair of hands.
Which made the 66-year-old's resignation as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary just over a month ago all the more shocking.
Healey's assessment of the government's much-delayed defence investment plan - that it fell "well short of what is required for defence and the country at this dangerous time" - was devastating and undoubtedly hastened Sir Keir's departure from Downing Street.
Now he's in charge of the funding not just of defence - but of every arm of government.
He replaces Rachel Reeves, who had served as Sir Keir's chancellor since Labour's 2024 landslide election win.
Loyal, and not someone who briefs against colleagues to journalists or indulges in political games, he has been around the top of the Labour party for three decades.
Live updates on this story
Burnham's policy choices reveal what kind of PM he wants to be
His resignation came days before Andy Burnham's pivotal by-election in Makerfield, adding to the sense that Sir Keir's premiership was falling apart.
Healey earned plaudits from across the political spectrum for resigning on a matter of principle.
He had clashed with Reeves, the woman he is now replacing, pointedly saying in is resignation letter that the Treasury had been "unwilling" to "commit the resources that the nation needs to defend the country at this time of rising threats".
His return to government in the most vital job of all in cabinet after the prime minister is an even bigger surprise than his resignation, given that his name had not been mentioned as a frontrunner in the increasingly feverish speculation about who Burnham would choose.
Sources told the BBC that Burnham and Healey "have the same outlook" on many of the prime minister's priorities, including reindustrialisation, the cost-of-living, and driving growth across the country.
The softly-spoken Yorkshireman has a remarkable record as someone who has been on the Labour frontbench almost continuously since 2001.
Born in Wakefield in 1960 and educated at Lady Lumley's Comprehensive School, Pickering, and Peter's School in York, he studied social and political science at Christ's College, Cambridge.
Before entering politics, he worked as a journalist, briefly editing Parliament's in-house magazine The House, before becoming a disability rights campaigner and trade union official.
He is married and has one son.
He first came into Parliament in Tony Blair's landslide general election in 1997 as MP for Wentworth, a former mining area north of Sheffield, which following boundary changes is now Rawmarsh and Conisbrough.
He retained the seat with a majority of 6,908 in the 2024 general election, with a Reform UK candidate in second place.
In the early 2000s, he held a string of ministerial posts, including housing, local government in the Blair and Gordon Brown governments.
He spent five years at Brown's Treasury where he oversaw policies such as the child trust funds and attempts to regenerate and devolve power - the Regional Development Agencies, later scrapped by the coalition government.
Speaking to the BBC's Political Thinking with Nick Robinson earlier this month, Healey said: "The Treasury's a paradox. You have some of the very best and brightest officials in the Treasury, but you have too often a Treasury orthodox that's a dead hand on dynamic government."
He added that maintaining financial stability was a key function of the Treasury but "also it can and it has to drive economic growth, raise levels of productivity, support business competition, investment for the for the future".
And he claimed the department "was in denial about the commitment that the UK has rightly made to NATO and to our people" to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP, which would not come until 2034/35 under current plans.
"The Treasury still often sees defence as a drain on public spending and not the driver of economic growth that we've demonstrated in two years," he told Nick Robinson.
Healey's other area of expertise is housing. He served as shadow housing secretary when Jeremy Corbyn was Labour leader, despite supporting a failed attempt to oust Corbyn in 2016.
Pundits had not touted Healey (right, dressed in a suit) as a frontrunner for the chancellor job
When Sir Keir was elected Labour leader in 2020, he made Healey shadow defence secretary, becoming defence secretary when Labour came to power four years later.
Healey was a staunch supporter of Ukraine in its war with Russia and made several trips to the country to meet President Zelensky.
At his first meeting with Nato allies, in September 2024, he said he was "confident" Labour could honour a commitment to increase defence spending and "make the decisions that allow us to set out a long-term plan to make our forces better equipped to fight and to deter the threats we face".
Healey also drove investment in housing for armed forces families , with a Â£9bn spending plan.
Despite his low key style, he proved capable of delivering stern warnings to the UK's enemies.
In April this year, he delivered a message to Russian President Vladimir Putin , in a briefing on "covert" operations by Russian sumbmarines, saying: "We see you.
"We see your activity over our cables and our pipelines, and you should know that any attempt to damage them will not be tolerated and will have serious consequences."
Following the announcement of the defence investment plan, he condemned what he called "Treasury trickery" and the lack of clarity on what new money the Ministry of Defence would get.
Healey also made clear that he wanted a clear plan to increase UK defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030.
Now he's the chancellor he will have the opportunity to set out that plan himself, and if he is true to his words, it can only mean more positive news for his successor as defence secretary.

title: Social care reform: The families hoping for change
description: As Andy Burnham outlines his aim to overhaul social care, BBC News speaks to the families caring for loved ones.
author: Rozina Sini, Jim Reed, Paul Gribben
content:
Emma Riley is a dental nurse from Manchester, as was her mother Carol before she retired
Andy Burnham has pledged to reform the adult social care system in England, meeting the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats to try to find "common ground" on the issue.
He wants an independent review of care to be brought forward by a year to 2027, as well as major reforms to pay and conditions for staff and the creation of a national care service.
But the prime minister said "difficult decisions" would have to be made on tax to fund sustainable change, adding that in an "ideal world" no-one should have to sell their home to pay for care.
BBC Your Voice has been speaking to families affected by what they see as shortfalls in the system.
Emma Riley has been caring for her mother Carol, who has dementia, since she lost her father 18 months ago.
"She's a cracking lady, still with a sense of humour but she's living with this awful condition," said Riley, from Manchester.
She is paying Â£34 an hour for a care company to come to the house three times a week, which she describes as a "huge chunk of money" although she is happy with the level of care.
Riley wants to keep her mum in the family home, but the caring commitments affect her job as a dental nurse.
She started applying to the local council for funding to support her mother at home at the beginning of the year, but six months on, she is still waiting for a final decision.
"It's not the social worker's fault, it is just the caseload," she said.
Riley called for more communication to help her navigate the system, adding: "I'm blindly going through it at the moment.
"Every day I'm just winging it but there's a human being upstairs."
Riley said she heard the prime minister's speech and it had left her feeling "quietly confident".
Burnham has announced that a review of social care by veteran Whitehall troubleshooter Baroness Casey would now be published next summer.
"I do think Baroness Casey will make the changes we need," Riley added.
Burnham doesn't rule out tax rises to fix social care
The Greenwood family in West Yorkshire say they have had to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for their mother, Mavis
Lisa Greenwood, from Halifax, West Yorkshire, said she would be supportive of the prime minister if he managed to change how the care sector operates.
"It does need changing and hopefully it will get better," she said.
Greenwood said her family is having to make "some very tough decisions" in caring for her mother, Mavis, who is 90 and in local respite care.
It is costing Â£1,305 a week, something Greenwood says the family "cannot sustain".
She said they now face the prospect of having to sell her mother's home, describing this as "very distressing".
Greenwood backs Burnham's proposal to increase pay in the sector and suggests it will help attract more staff.
"Carers do need to be paid more," she said. "There are some fantastic people doing the job on little wages."
Greenwood told the BBC's Your Voice that both her parents had worked "all their lives saving for the future".
"Yet here we are in a situation of stress not knowing how we are going to continue with mum in the home," she added.
"We can't give up our jobs, we need to work to pay our bills."
Sophie and her father Stephen, who died in 2024 when she was just 16
Sophie Daniels was 16 when her father died in 2024 as a result of stage 4 glioblastoma, a highly aggressive brain tumour.
The 18-year-old felt that there was a lack of support for her family. Along with her mother and sister, she looked after her father at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire, as "social care provision was incredibly limited".
Daniels said: "We hardly had any help and we were left to figure things out ourselves.
"Thankfully, charities helped us with that but towards the end my mum had to give up work to care for my dad."
She said that one of the biggest practical challenges her family faced was a lack of a lifting service to help him move around the house.
"He fell fairly frequently and a lack of lifting service meant that our dad was forced to either wait for hours on the floor for an ambulance or for us to try and use techniques to pull my dad up."
Andy Burnham made his speech at a north London care home, where he spoke to some of the residents
Steve West, from Wakefield, West Yorkshire, cared for his mother for many years before taking the difficult decision to place her in a care home. She died earlier this year.
West, 64, said he was "frustrated hearing the same issues that need fixing being discussed by each new government".
Listening to the prime minister's speech, he said that a proposed national care service "could give focus, but its remit needs to be confirmed".
"I think a cross-party approach would be a benefit as the plans would take a few terms of parliament at least and then to maintain the benefits for years to come," he added.
He said when caring for his mother, the biggest challenge was "knowing who to speak to" and "dealing with several health bodies", sometimes having to repeat her medical history several times.
"She got progressively worse and I remember one time sitting in a car park for an hour-and-a-half trying to get an emergency social worker," he said, adding that "having a system that is unified would be a massive help".
West believes the prime minister "needs to focus on one or two big-ticket items - those that will have the biggest impact".
He said if relatives caring for loved ones were paid at similar rates to private companies, "perhaps more people would feel they were able to provide support" as they would not be negatively impacted by cutting work hours or leaving their jobs.
John Barry was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died from the disease in 2024. Pictured here with his wife Jeanette.
Jeanette Barry from Essex was married to her husband John for 42 years before he was diagnosed with dementia in 2018.
The former policeman was moved to a local care home as his needs became more complex.
"At one point he was roaming the streets at night because he thought he was still on duty," said Barry.
"I couldn't keep him in the house, so at 2am or 3am I was having to follow him to make sure he was alright."
She paid Â£2,000 a month in care home fees out of her husband's police pension, on top of local authority funding, although she didn't "begrudge a penny of that money" as he was well looked after.
She says she was told by one social worker that she would have to remortgage her house or her husband would be moved to another care home, but he was later reassessed and qualified for more financial support.
"I had to think twice before putting my heating on," she says. "It was a horrible, terrible time for the family."
Barry, whose husband died two years ago, said she doesn't have much faith in politicians to make the social care system work, but noted the prime minister has experience of the matter as his father has Alzheimer's.
"They all make promises but then they never do anything," she said.
"I have slightly more confidence in Andy Burnham because he has personal experience of dementia but how is he going to pay for it?"

title: Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar set to become a minister in Burnham's government
description: It would mean Sarwar leaving the Scottish Parliament and his leader role, then taking up a seat in the House of Lords.
author: Chris Mason, Catherine Lyst
content:
Anas Sarwar had called for Sir Keir Starmer to resign in February
Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar is set to stand down to become a minister in Andy Burnham's government.
It would mean Sarwar leaving the Scottish Parliament and his leader role, then taking up a seat in the House of Lords.
Sarwar publicly called for Sir Keir Starmer to resign in February, provoking a political near-death experience for the then prime minister.
It is thought Sarwar, who has led the Scottish Labour Party since 2021, will become a business minister.
Sarwar ministerial role sees promotion of another Starmer critic
He was at the event in London last Friday when Burnham became the new Labour Party leader.
Scottish Labour won just 17 seats out of 129 in the Scottish Parliament elections in May.
Andy Burnham still has a raft of ministerial appointments to make
Following the Holyrood election defeat Sarwar promised to stay on as leader in Scotland but his appointment as a minister at Westminster is expected to create a leadership vacancy.
Deputy leader of Scottish Labour and MSP Jackie Baillie is expected to step up to cover Sarwar's role ahead of a contest.
There will not however be a by-election for Sarwar's Holyrood seat as he was elected via the regional list.
Monica Lennon, who had been in the Scottish Parliament for a decade but was not re-elected in May, is the next name on the Glasgow list.
As of last year, new rules prevent politicians from sitting at both Westminster and Holyrood at the same time .
In May, as reported by The Herald , external , when asked if he would ever take up a seat in the House of Lords, Sarwar said: "No. I'm focused on being first minister of this great country."
He added: "My only commitment, my only focus, is serving my constituents in Glasgow and serving the great people of this country, if I get the honour of being first minister."
After Sir Keir's resignation in June, when asked if he planned to serve as party leader for the full five-year Holyrood term he said: "That is my intention.
"I'm hungry for the fight ahead and I want to play my full part in making sure this country never ends up in the hands of Nigel Farage and Reform."
Sarwar made last-minute decision to call for Starmer's resignation
Sarwar says he will 'absolutely' stay on as Labour leader
Douglas Alexander to remain Scottish Secretary as Burnham confirms cabinet
When Burnham became prime minister on Monday, Sarwar hailed him for his "bold Labour vision".
Former Greater Manchester mayor Burnham appointed his cabinet on Monday night, but a raft of ministerial appointments are still to come.
BBC Scotland Westminster correspondent Paris Gourtsoyannis said Scottish Labour parliamentarians appeared to have been blindsided by the news.
An MSP called Sarwar's decision "bizarre", while a senior Scottish Labour MP said it was "absolutely mad. I cannot begin to fathom the logic of it."
As a Scottish Labour peer, Sarwar would be entitled to attend meetings of the Scottish PLP at Westminster - a group which earlier this year collectively refused to back their leader's call for Keir Starmer to resign as prime minister.
Scotland's First Minister and SNP leader John Swinney wished Sarwar well in his "exciting new job" however he was critical of Burnham.
Speaking to BBC Radio Scotland's Breakfast programme, Swinney said: "It is a terrible look for Andy Burnham because the new PM has made a great play of essentially improving people's perceptions of politics and politicians.
"And to make one of his first decisions a decision to take the Labour leader in Scotland, who has just led the Labour Party to their worst result in the Scottish Parliament elections in the history of the Scottish parliament elections, and give him a job for life in the House of Lords and a job in the UK government is in my view a very, very strange way of trying to rebuild the confidence of the public in politics."
Reform UK's Scotland deputy leader Thomas Kerr said: "Only weeks ago, Anas Sarwar stood before the people of Glasgow asking for their trust and insisting that his future was here in Scotland. Today, those same voters will rightly feel betrayed.
"Throughout the election campaign, he dismissed suggestions that he had ambitions elsewhere and claimed his focus was on serving Scotland.
"Now, at the first opportunity, he has walked away from the very people who placed their faith in him."
And Scottish Green Party co-leader Gillian Mackay accused Sarwar of being a "chancer" who had "gone from promising to scrap the House of Lords to taking a seat in it".
She added: "By grabbing a place on the unelected red benches, he's ensured that he gets all of the power and privilege without having to worry about what voters might think.
"It is clearly not right or fair for politicians who have been rejected by the country to end up as law makers for the rest of their lives safe in the knowledge that there is nothing anyone can do to stop them."
Who will replace Anas Sarwar?
We discuss the likely contenders vying to succeed Sarwar as Scottish Labour leader.
Jim Murphy, who was Scottish Labour leader from 2014 to 2015, told BBC News: "If it's confirmed I think it's good news for him [Sarwar] personally but it probably, on balance, strengthens the government.
"It will open up a vacancy, of course, for leader of the Scottish Labour Party."
He said Andy Burnham had a maximum three years until the next election and had appointed people he felt could deliver quickly.
Murphy added: "He's come to a judgment that Anas, as part of a wider team, can do that.
"That will be difficult for him [Sarwar]. He will have to get up to speed very quickly but congratulations to him."

title: Rare breeding bat found roosting near South Yorkshire reservoir
description: The Nathusius' pipistrelle is believed to be the first confirmed discovery of its kind in the area.
author: Naj Modak
content:
Mithusius Pipistrelle is classed as "nearly threatened" in the UK
A rare species of breeding bat has been found roosting in woodland near a reservoir.
The Nathusius' pipistrelle has been confirmed at a Yorkshire Water site near Sheffield, the first time it had been recorded in South Yorkshire.
Environmental DNA (eDNA) collected from a bat box in March indicated the animal's presence, and in April one was physically spotted at another nearby bat box.
Lead ecologist at Yorkshire Water, Sean Davey, said: "The bat boxes on the Sheffield site were installed only nine months prior - so it's encouraging to see them being quickly adopted by multiple bat species."
The bat boxes were funded by Yorkshire Water's species conservation programme and installed in 2025. They were designed to mimic the natural features bats used for roosting, enhancing their habitats and helping bat populations to thrive on its sites.
Davey said DNA swabs were trialled by ecologists from Yorkshire Water and the South Yorkshire Bat Group.
He said: "Bat boxes and other known roost sites were swabbed to collect eDNA samples, revealing the presence of the rare migrant bat."
Using eDNA swabs was a "potentially useful monitoring tool" for ecologists
The company said monitoring the bat boxes at the site helped confirm the conservation measures were working and could highlight "unexpected and valuable" results, like the Nathusius' pipistrelle.
It said using eDNA swabs was a "potentially useful monitoring tool" for ecologists as data could be easily missed in 'one-off' surveys like a visual bat box check.
These techniques could more widely increase knowledge of species' distributions, helping effective conservation to be targeted in the right place, it said.
Working alongside South Yorkshire Bat Group and Yorkshire Water, biodiversity intelligence company NatureMetrics analysed eDNA collected from bat boxes and detected Nathusius' pipistrelle â?? one of the UK's rarer rarest breeding bat species, which is known to migrate long distances between the UK and Europe.
The finding was later confirmed in follow-up surveys, marking the first confirmed roost of the species in South Yorkshire.
According to the Bat Conservation Trust, the species is similar in appearance to, but slightly larger than, the common bat but with longer fur on its back.
Product ecologist at Nature Metrics, Dr George Muscatt, said the eDNA was "tiny traces or fingerprints of DNA that species in that ecosystem have left behind".
He said previously the team would have to climb the trees at night to "try to visually identify a species occupying a bat roost", which was time consuming.
"By taking a surface swab approach, we've been able to monitor a far larger number of bat boxes in a very short space of time," he said.

title: Draft dark skies guidance drawn up for the Highlands
description: The plan to reduce light pollution could be put out for public consultation at a later date.
author: Steven McKenzie
content:
Highland Council has said its region has some of Europe's darkest skies
Highland Council has produced draft guidance aimed at reducing light pollution to give stargazers clearer views of the night sky.
Officials said other benefits of minimising outdoor lighting included lower carbon emissions and energy costs.
The guidance would support communities wishing to set up dark sky sites, which are locations with little or no light pollution.
Builders of major developments in, or near, dark sky sites would be required to carry out a lighting assessment to justify the need for exterior lights.
More stories from the Highlands and Islands
News from the Highlands and Islands on BBC Sounds
Councillors meeting next week have been asked to approve the draft guidance , external .
It would then be put out for public consultation before a finalised version of the document was produced.
The guidance could form part of Highland Council's proposed Highland Local Development Plan (HLDP), which is due to be published next year.
The HLDP would set out areas of the region to be zoned for housing or other developments.
A view of the night sky from Invermoriston taken on 13 August
In a report, officials said the proposed guidance would encourage best practice by minimising exterior lighting to only what was necessary for safety and security.
They said: "There are environmental benefits in terms of reduced emissions and lower adverse impacts on humans and wildlife, financial benefits in reduced energy usage and bills, and tourism economy benefits in terms of retaining and enhancing visitors' ability to enjoy the night sky."
In the report, planting trees and adding fencing have been suggested as ways of reducing the glare of outside lights.
Officials acknowledged that some communities would prefer to have exterior lighting for safety reasons.
The local authority has previously said the Highlands, which has large, sparsely populated areas, offered astronomy fans some of the darkest skies in Europe .
In 2024, the Isle of Rum, which is in the Highland Council area, was named Scotland's first International Dark Sky Sanctuary by the organisation DarkSky International.

title: Discord ordered to suspend livestreams in Brazil following teen suicide
description: Discord told the BBC it was "thoughtfully reviewing" the order by Brazil's data protection agency and it was "committed to user safety"
author: Laura Cress
content:
Brazil's data protection authority (ANPD) has ordered Discord to suspend its livestreaming feature after a teenage girl was allegedly encouraged to take her own life in a broadcast on the platform.
The messaging service allows people to create and join groups based on their interests, with users able to enter voice or video calls in real time through Discord's "Go Live" feature.
The investigation by the ANPD began on 7 August after the death of a 13-year-old girl, who was reportedly pressured to end her life by others in the Discord server - or group - she was in.
Discord told the BBC it was "thoughtfully reviewing" the ANPD's order and is "committed to user safety".
"Groups or individuals who promote or encourage violence have no place on Discord," a spokesperson said.
"We swiftly investigated and shut down the private, invite-only server involved shortly after its creation and continue to cooperate with law enforcement in its investigation."
According to Reuters , external , the ANPD said it found Discord lacks â??real-time â access to livestream content, which prevents automated violation detection.
The site, which can be accessed on desktop or as a mobile app, has over 200 million monthly active users, and is popular with gamers.
Discord's spokesperson said in its investigation, evidence was found that the criminal activity "was coordinated on other platforms before the Discord server was created" as well as continuing "after the individuals involved were banned from Discord".
Five teenagers have reportedly been arrested in connection to the teenage girl's death.
Discord now has three days to comply with the suspension and can appeal the decision within 10 business days.
The platform faces potential fines of â??up to 50m reais ($9.67m) per â violation.
The ANPD said the suspension will remain in place until Discord proves it has implemented "adequate protective measures for minors", which may include age verification checks.
In August 2024, the social media platform X was banned in Brazil after failing to pay existing fines and to meet a deadline set by a Supreme Court judge to name a new legal representative in the country.
It was unbanned by the Supreme Court in October 2024 after it complied with court orders by paying fines totalling 28m reais ($5.1m; Â£3.8m) and agreed to appoint a local representative, as required by Brazilian law.

title: How parents and pupils took on 'cruel', 'authoritarian' schools - and won
description: Discipline at an academy trust went too far - parents, pupils and former teachers tell BBC Panorama.
author: Richard Bilton
content:
Amelia's mother, Kayley (r), says strict school policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill
To avoid getting into trouble, 14-year-old Amelia says she decided to stop drinking water at school so she would not need the toilet.
Her school, Camborne Science and International Academy in Cornwall, had introduced strict disciplinary policies, which included limiting toilet visits during classes, according to pupils and former teachers.
New discipline rules were implemented when the school was taken over in January 2024 by the Athena Learning Trust, which runs six secondary schools in Devon and Cornwall.
Amelia's mother, Kayley, believes these strict policies resulted in her daughter becoming ill from a series of serious infections caused by not drinking.
Hundreds of parents, including Kayley, have campaigned against the way Athena runs its schools.
Across Devon and Cornwall, there have been public meetings, school-gate protests and online petitions. Local MPs and councillors have also backed concerned parents.
The opposition to Athena now appears to have paid off - with the trust announcing last month that it was planning to disband and transfer all its schools to other trusts.
It said that trustees had "listened carefully to feedback" and recognised the "clear need for change".
BBC Panorama has spoken to nearly 100 pupils, parents and former teachers from Athena schools, who say levels of discipline went too far. Many pupils and parents queued to talk to us at two town hall meetings we arranged.
The way the schools had been run was "authoritarian" and "cruel", some said.
"You're constantly scared you're going to do something wrong," one student with ADHD told us, while a former music teacher said the strict discipline had meant his lessons were taught in silence.
Camborne Science and International Academy is one of six schools run by the Athena Learning Trust
Athena is not the only academy trust that has enforced strict discipline.
There are those who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils - and exam results at Athena-run schools have improved.
About 20% of the school day in England is lost to bad behaviour, the government says.
The benefits of a "high level of strictness" is that students understand what is expected of them, says the government advisor on behaviour in schools in England, Tom Bennett.
Commenting generally, rather than on individual academies, he told us that pupils soon realise they have to get into the habit of meeting expectations.
However, there is growing concern that punitive disciplinary practices at some schools in England are damaging children.
Britainâ??s Strictest Schools
How much discipline is too much? Panorama investigates the academy trust where classrooms are silent and pupils can be sent to detention for looking out of the window.
Watch on iPlayer now or on Monday 3 August at 20:00 on BBC One.
Athena's secondary schools are attended by about 6,500 children. In the past three years, more than 500 children have left to be educated at home, according to Cornwall and Devon county councils.
Amelia is one of them.
While at Camborne, Amelia would often come home with the bottle of water she had left with in the morning still full.
When Kayley asked Amelia why, she says her daughter would reply that she had not drunk anything all day, "so I wouldn't need to go to the toilet".
Camborne has strict rules around toilet visits during lessons.
Pupils were not allowed to go to the toilet in the first or last 15 minutes of a lesson, and were only allowed to go in the middle of a lesson at the teacher's discretion, pupils and former teachers told us.
On school days, Amelia would only drink after school and in the evening. Kayley believes her daughter's fear of breaking the rules ended up making her ill.
"She's now on antibiotics, she's had water infections, she has got scarring on her kidneys because of this," Kayley says.
Amelia says her time at Camborne "makes me feel ill, even thinking of it".
Athena told Panorama that staff work hard to "support children to remain in education" and "support access to toilets during lessons" through professional staff judgement.
Former teacher at Launceston, Brian Maywood, initially welcomed the changes brought in by Athena
Academies are independent, state-funded schools, that receive their funding directly from central government, rather than through a local authority. They have independent control over their own admissions, curriculum and staff pay.
There are no academy trusts in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland, but more than 80% of secondary schools in England are now run by them.
Multi-academy trusts like Athena oversee a network of schools. Athena's reports from the regulator, Ofsted, have mostly been positive.
Brian Maywood used to be the head of Launceston College in north Cornwall and was an English teacher there when Athena took over.
Initially he welcomed the trust's highly disciplined approach, and was pleased the school was "moving into a new way of learning".
But his opinion quickly shifted, he says, once he witnessed how the children were treated, calling it a "dictatorship".
The way students were spoken to at times "made me really, really uncomfortable", he adds.
He left the school last summer because of these reasons, he says.
It was the same for the former head of art, Estelle Pears.
"There is discipline and then there is being oppressed," she says. "It sounds dramatic, but that's what it became.
"If you're frightened of moving a pencil on a desk because you will get a sanction, that's beyond discipline."
Ieuan Horgan, who taught music at Launceston, said his classes had to be in silence
Former Athena teachers who spoke to Panorama said they were forced to uphold the strict rules by the trust and that some made little sense.
Ieuan Horgan says his music lessons had to be taught in silence.
"At the start of the lesson, I would go through how to play the musical notation, and then the lesson would just be silent focus on trying to learn this musical notation," he says.
"They pushed for 100% distraction and disruption-free lessons - and 100% silent focus - in a music lesson."
Pupils have told Panorama they could be punished for minor offences and Bethany, who has just finished her GCSEs at Camborne, describes the strict and regimented approach as "demoralising" and "like you're being talked to like you were a primary school kid".
Athena schools have a two-strike policy: a warning for one mistake, sent out of the class for the second. Students then go to what is called "reflection" - a room where they work in silence from workbooks.
At Launceston College there were about 1,000 cases a month of pupils being sent to "reflection" rooms between September 2025 and March 2026, according to figures released by the trust.
Athena says reflection rooms are "supervised environments" where "students continue their learning independently".
It says it does not have a rigid two strikes policy and the "vast majority of students spend little or no time in these spaces". Students are not normally punished for isolated minor issues, it adds.
Jack, who has special educational needs, was regularly sent to reflection and suspended, his mother says
Some parents say children with special educational needs and disabilities are disproportionately affected by Athena's strict policies.
April, whose son Jack has special educational needs and has just finished his GCSEs at Ilfracombe Academy, says he was sent to reflection countless times.
He could not cope with the regimented environment, she says.
"Just to look out the window to refocus, that's not harming any of the other children or their education within the room - but that's enough to be sent out, because that's him not focusing on the teacher."
Jack was also suspended - sent home from school - dozens of times. He is far from alone.
The suspension rate at Ilfracombe Academy was almost five times higher than the average in England, according to government figures for 2023 to 2025. At Camborne, it was about five times higher than the average and three times higher at Launceston, according to the same figures.
Athena says suspensions are reserved for "serious or repeated breaches of behaviour expectations" and that rates have fallen significantly in the past year.
Zara says her autistic daughter Hannah, who has hearing difficulties and attends Ilfracombe Academy, was repeatedly removed from class
April and Jack's concerns were echoed at our town-hall events. More than half of the dozens of parents and pupils who turned up were concerned about the impact on students with special educational needs.
Finn, a student at Camborne with ADHD, says it was a difficult environment for neurodiverse pupils. "You're constantly scared that you're going to do something wrong," he says.
Faye, whose son has special educational needs and attends Pool Academy, says he had spent 96 hours in reflection the past school year. "Day in, day out, he feels like he's failing," she says.
And Zara says her autistic daughter Hannah, who has hearing difficulties and attends Ilfracombe Academy, was repeatedly removed from class because her needs were not recognised.
"Behaviour is just put down to persistent defiance and bad behaviour, and they're punished for it," she says. "It's never recognised as being linked to their disabilities."
Athena told us that children with special educational needs are "not routinely sanctioned for behaviours associated with their needs".
A lot of the anger we heard in Devon and Cornwall is, we were told, down to the lack of accountability.
Academy trusts do not have any supervision from local councils, meaning only central government can intervene.
One of the biggest weaknesses of the trust system is that it complicates the complaints process, says education journalist Laura McInerney, who co-founded Teacher Tapp, an app designed to track educators' wellbeing, classroom practices, and opinions on education policy.
If parents are not satisfied with a specific school's response, she says, they have to contact the trust, which could be miles way, and which "you may or may not hear from in anything other than a letter".
The government says parents can take complaints about academy trusts to the Department for Education.
Across England, there is growing concern about punitive disciplinary practices in schools.
The BBC's File on 4 Investigates recently found that a school in Wakefield, West Yorkshire, put a pupil in an isolation booth away from the classroom for more than half an academic year.
Pupil put in isolation booth for more than half a school year, BBC learns
A safeguarding review last year also found an east London school's zero-tolerance policy involved pupils being routinely humiliated by shouting and prioritised control above all else, leaving some children with lasting psychological harm.
A team at law firm Leigh Day is now investigating potential legal claims on behalf of 50 families who believe their children may have been subjected to excessive or inappropriate disciplinary measures while at school.
However, there are many who argue that education built on tough discipline and high expectations can benefit pupils.
The government's advisor on behaviour, Tom Bennett, told us that discipline is vital, including for children with special educational needs.
"If you've got, for example, ADHD or an anxiety disorder, what you need more than anybody else is a calm, safe, dignified environment. Otherwise, you'll be massively distracted by the environment round about you," Bennett says.
Bethany says the Athena trust has caused "incredible harm"
In Devon and Cornwall, parents appear to have won in their campaign against Athena.
In May, the head of the trust, who implemented the tough discipline, resigned.
Last month, the trust announced it was planning to disband.
In a statement, Athena said it had "listened carefully" and recognised the "clear need for change". It said it would work with the Department for Education to "identify alternative trusts" to which the schools could transfer.
Until then, Athena will keep running the schools.
The Department for Education told Panorama the allegations about Athena are "serious and concerning" and that it is "taking robust action to make sure the trust improves" ahead of the schools transferring.
The trust is now "subject to enhanced monitoring" to make sure its "approach to pupil behaviour is reasonable and proportionate", it says.
Bethany says the school has caused "incredible harm".
"They need to change the way that they're thinking they can teach students as a one-size-fits-all."

title: Australian state to begin gun buyback after Bondi Beach attack
description: New South Wales, where the attack took place, will offer gun owners cash to give up their firearms.
author: Dearbail Jordan
content:
Fifteen people were shot dead at a Jewish festival on Bondi Beach
Australia's most populous state will launch a gun buyback scheme later this year, becoming the first to offer cash in exchange for firearms following the Bondi Beach terror attack.
Gun owners in New South Wales (NSW) will be offered up to AUS$1,000 (Â£523) to hand over eligible handguns, shotguns and rifles from 2 November.
Australian authorities had pledged sweeping firearm law reforms after 15 people were shot dead at a Jewish festival on Sydney's Bondi Beach, which is located in NSW, last December.
The state's Premier Chris Minns said on Saturday: "We want those guns handed in, compensated for and safely destroyed."
He said the move could see hundreds of thousands of guns surrendered.
Gun ownership reforms already introduced by the state mean individuals can only own four firearms - although some people, such as farmers and sports shooters, can own a maximum of 10.
The scheme will be offered to those who have more weapons than permitted by the new rules, or who are no longer covered by a licence - with terms having been reduced from five years to two.
The scheme will be implemented in two phases. The first - from the start of November - covers types of handguns, shotguns and rifles.
Those handing over a revolver, for example, will be paid AUS$1,000, while an air rifle will fetch AUS$450.
The second phase will begin early next year and cover "higher-value firearms" valued above AUS$3,000, capped at AUS$10,000.
The National Gun BuyBack Scheme is being jointly funded by New South Wales and the federal government.
Businesses will be able to receive up to AUS$25,000 in support to help them adjust to the reforms, with help also offered to gun-dealers.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said: "We must do everything we can to make sure the antisemitic terrorist attack in Bondi doesn't happen again.
"That includes meaningful nationwide gun reform."
On 14 December last year, 15 people including a 10-year-old girl and a Holocaust survivor were killed as Hanukkah celebrations took place along Australia's famed beachfront.
Australian authorities had initially planned a nationwide gun buyback, though plans have been delayed over funding and questions about how it would be implemented.

title: Surrey families to get back to school support from council fund
description: From September, uniforms will be limited to three items requiring a school logo.
author: Cash Murphy
content:
The Crisis and Resilience Fund is a three-year UK government funding programme administered by SCC
A charity has been awarded Â£100,000 to help Surrey families experiencing financial hardship buy back to school essentials, including uniforms items, for the upcoming year.
While a new law in September means that parents in England will have to buy fewer branded items of school uniform, costs remain high.
Surrey County Council (SCC) has given charity Stripey Stork the money to expand its School Days scheme which helps families access essential school items.
Nicola Dawes, chief executive at Stripey Stork, said families in need would "simply go without essential school items or be forced into debt" without this support.
In 2025, the charity's School Days Programme supported 7,503 children from 4,116 families
The funding comes from the Â£7.1m Crisis and Resilience Fund, a government-run scheme which provides local authorities with funding to help low-income households on a multi-year basis.
Last year, Stripey Stork supported 7,503 Surrey children from 4,116 families.
This latest funding will enable the charity to support around 8,500 children over the next 12 months.
Councillor Mark Nuti, SCC cabinet member for health and communities, said this money will help Stripey Stork to "reach even more families across Surrey with practical support at a time when it is needed most".

title: Burnham admits cost of living help is not enough and hints at further support
description: The PM has announced a rake of measures to help people since taking office three weeks ago.
author: Felicity Hannah, Emer Moreau
content:
The prime minister said he understood that his cost-of-living announcements were not enough to meaningfully help people
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he accepts his announcements aimed at tackling the cost of living are not enough on their own and hinted at further support.
Burnham told BBC's Wake up to Money he will deliver an "accumulation of smaller things" that "combine to take the pressure down" on household budgets.
He spoke of an overhaul of train fares and "more public control" of energy, water and housing but did not give details on how he would bring this about.
Burnham has made a number of announcements to help people with the cost of living since taking office, including the removal of VAT from domestic electricity bills and bringing forward an already planned end to 'subscription traps' .
Asked whether the changes he had announced were not significant to people struggling, he said: "I can accept criticism that this isn't enough, because I wouldn't say it's enough.
"But I take an approach to politics where I do what I can, when I can. Just take that little bit of pressure off and address an issue that you know needs addressing.
"It's not the end of the story," he added.
The prime minister, who is embarking on a tour of the UK while Parliament is in recess, said he believed "more public control of essential services" such as water, energy and housing, "would mean we could get to a more substantial answer to the cost of living crisis".
On water, he said it would not be easy to reverse the privatisation of water companies in England and Wales that took place in the 1980s.
"But very much, I'm looking at what can be done. Same with energy."
He also said that, following the return of rail operators to public ownership, he wanted to "remodel the rail fares so that we can get more public benefit for people".
It comes as the government said on Wednesday that people living within 1,600ft (500m) of new upgraded electricity pylons and substations across Britain will receive a Â£250 annual discount on their bills for a decade.
Andy Burnham: Wake Up to Money
The prime minister tells Wake Up to Money that the increase to national insurance has "added pressure" to businesses.
Burnham told the BBC he has asked Chancellor John Healey to look at what the government can do further on the cost of living in the upcoming Budget, on 28 October, and that Healey has said it will be his "main focus".
Healey has made it clear he will oversee "strong fiscal discipline" â?? which will limit how much the government has to spend.
One major think tank recently warned that he will have to raise taxes or cut spending to meet Burnham's pledges on defence and the cost of living.
Labour's manifesto pledge was to not increase taxes for working people â?? including income tax, VAT and National Insurance Contributions (NICs) - which Burnham has said he will uphold.
He will likely face pressure to address rising costs for businesses, after previous budgets under Rachel Reeves saw employer's national insurance and minimum wages go up.
Last month Burnham said pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England would be given a 20% cut to business rates from April, calling it a "first step" to help the industry.
He told the BBC he accepted the national insurance hike had added pressure on businesses, and that the government would look at business rates "more broadly".
Burnham said: "I would like to bring down the cost of doing businesses. I want to make high streets more vibrant across the country. I know that cannot be done by simply wishing it."
But he said he did not want to "at this point, start making commitments".
"Those are for the Budget."

title: Soldiers praised for helping crews tackle wildfires in south Wales
description: About 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment have been involved in the operation.
author: Mark Palmer, Nicholas Bourne
content:
Soldiers from 10 Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment are among 200 military personnel helping with wildfires in south Wales
A chief fire officer has praised soldiers for supporting crews tackling wildfires in south Wales.
Fin Monahan said South Wales Fire and Rescue Service was under severe pressure and very grateful to seven other fire services and the military for help.
About 200 members of the Queen's Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment, with support from 22 Royal Engineers, Royal Logistics Corp and Army helicopters have been been involved.
Crews from London, Cumbria and elsewhere have also been providing support.
Monahan told the BBC the UK and Welsh governments took "a very serious step" in bringing in the military but the "extra capacity" was needed as crews fought dozens of fires across the country.
He said his firefighters have "very specialist skills" to tackle wildfires with military assistance enabling him to "focus all of that in the right place".
Soldiers have been providing logistical support, including water distribution, to assist firefighters and specialist responders.
Monahan described the soldiers as "doing an utterly phenomenal job digging trenches and also helping us build fire breaks".
"That has liberated lots of our firefighters to go and do their more specialist skills of firefighting."
Crews from Hay-on-Wye Fire Station have been sharing photos of their efforts on their Facebook page
In south Wales, about 14 separate fires were being tackled by crews on Sunday.
Mid and West Wales Fire Rescue and Service said crews were dealing with blazes at Rhandirmwyn and Ammanford in Carmarthenshire and Hay-on-Wye and Brecon in Powys on Sunday.
They have also attended fires in Gorseinon, Swansea, and Tenby, Pembrokeshire, as well as an incident involving smoke in Llanelli, Carmarthenshire.
Chris Bryant, MP for Rhondda and Ogmore, said a fire in Treherbert, Rhondda Cynon Taf, had been "appalling" and he thanked crews from London who had provided assistance.
"Thankfully, there are fire engines from all over the UK and two helicopters have been in place all afternoon.
"I'm immensely impressed by the fire workers. But this can't be our new normal," he said, in a post on X , external on Saturday.
Monahan praised the Royal Logistics Corps and Royal Engineers in ensuring crews had water to tackle the fires.
"The Welsh water system is under pressure, so they're moving vast quantities of water from areas that we have it into areas where we're fighting the fire, so that we don't put too much pressure on the water system," he said.
"That's something people probably aren't aware of."
He also said the national emergency fire alert issued by the UK government to people's mobile phones in England and Wales on Friday was "absolutely necessary".
But he expressed disappointment that some people still did not appreciate the dangers.
"Even after that transmission, I stopped and found someone who was burning tyres underneath a tree.
"This is irresponsible behaviour," he said.

title: How AI is changing jobs in the Philippines' outsourcing industry
description: AI is reshaping the Philippines' outsourcing industry, raising questions over the future of the industry.
author: Suranjana Tewari
content:
The Philippines is known as the call centre capital of the world
For 15 years, single mother Lisa made a living from content writing.
She began writing straight out of college, freelanced for years and eventually followed a path taken by many young Filipinos: joining a multinational in the country's booming outsourcing industry.
Lisa says she never felt the need to use artificial intelligence (AI) in her work.
"I can say that I am able to do my job, I meet deadlines. In my opinion, there is no need for [AI]," she told the BBC.
Eight months into her latest role, and one month before the position was due to become permanent, she was made redundant.
In the months before, Lisa says a public relations agency had been tasked with producing AI-generated material that she and her colleagues were asked to edit. She says her skills were used to train the AI on the company writing style.
"I feel like I dug my own grave," she says. "We were the ones who trained the artificial intelligence that replaced us."
Lisa, not her real name, is one of several former outsourcing employees the BBC spoke to who asked to remain anonymous. They signed confidentiality agreements in return for severance pay, and fear that speaking publicly could hurt their chances of finding work in an industry which has a small network.
Their experiences offer an insight into a question confronting emerging economies like the Philippines: what happens when AI begins to automate the jobs that helped lift millions of people into the middle classes?
Every evening around 5pm, streams of workers wearing company lanyards spill out of high-rise offices in the district of Cubao in Manila.
It's one of several areas of the capital where multinational companies have premises â?? providing all sorts of outsourcing work including call centres, accounting, software development and marketing copy services for clients thousands of miles away.
For over two decades, these business districts have symbolised one of the Philippines' biggest economic success stories.
Beginning in the early 2000s, the country was promoted as an English-speaking alternative to India for what's called business process outsourcing (BPO).
Successive governments offered tax incentives, invested in infrastructure and encouraged multinational companies to set up large operations.
Global groups like Accenture, Concentrix and Teleperformance built sprawling campuses, employing hundreds of thousands of Filipinos.
Today, the outsourcing industry employs roughly 1.9 million people, and generates $40bn (Â£30.1bn) in revenues every year, accounting for about 10% of the Philippines' economy.
But experts say the industry is disproportionately vulnerable to the impact of AI.
The outsourcing industry employs about 1.9 million people in the Philippines
The International Labour Organization estimates that 12.7 million Filipinos - more than one in four workers - are employed in occupations exposed to generative AI, the highest share in South East Asia.
The organisation expects many roles to change rather than disappear but the types of service jobs that people do in the Philippines leaves it particularly at risk.
Jack Madrid, president of the IT and Business Process Association of the Philippines (IBPAP), admits that AI is being adopted by the sector.
More than two-thirds of IBPAP's members are already running AI pilots, he says.
"Agentic AI has the potential to automate at a much more accelerated pace," Madrid says. "Obviously, there's a layer of jobs that are automatable or have been automated."
But he adds that the vast majority of affected workers have been redeployed within the same organisations.
Madrid says any weakness in hiring reflects more than the impact of AI.
"We've seen a slowdown in investment decisions on whether certain job functions or processes should be offshored," he says, pointing to slower global demand and uncertainty over how companies will ultimately deploy the technology.
Even so, he acknowledges the challenge. "We cannot do enough to be prepared," he says. "The importance of reskilling" cannot be overstated.
Mary, another former content writer whose name we've changed, says her employer encouraged the use of AI as a productivity tool.
Instead of making her job easier, she says it created additional responsibilities.
"We had to edit more, fact-check more because the data AI produced was inaccurate," she says. "Technically it was more work for us."
Like Lisa, she was later made redundant.
Companies are under pressure to implement AI, to reduce costs and increase productivity, experts say.
Teleperformance, the world's largest call centre operator and one of the Philippines' biggest private employers, has said AI offers an opportunity to augment rather than replace its workforce.
The company expects AI to handle routine interactions while human agents move into more complex roles.
Teleperformance has also said it plans to retrain employees.
Accenture has similarly said that generative AI will reshape almost every job rather than eliminate positions.
The firm has promised to invest billions of dollars in AI capabilities and workforce training.
Concentrix - which is the biggest outsourcing firm in the Philippines - says its AI systems should remain under human oversight and has committed to training employees in the new technology.
Some Filipino managers are uneasy about AI and want to slow down adoption, according to Paul Quintos, from the University of the Philippines-Diliman.
They are concerned about how much of the domestic workforce might be displaced.
"But there's tremendous pressure from foreign clients to adopt AI," he says. "It's a major cost-cutting measure."
Philippine outsourcing companies compete directly with rivals in India and elsewhere for contracts from multinational corporations.
Increasingly, those clients expect suppliers not only to provide cheaper labour, but also to integrate AI into the services they deliver.
The BBC spoke to employees who say they trained AI before being let go
Despite hundreds of billions of dollars being invested globally in AI, Quintos says there is still limited evidence about how much productivity many workplace tools actually deliver.
"There is a term called 'AI washing'," he says.
Some layoffs are presented as being driven by AI when companies are in fact responding to weaker demand or slowing economic conditions, Quintos says.
Attributing redundancies to AI, he adds, can make restructuring appear like technological progress rather than a response to market conditions.
Labour groups have told the BBC that existing employment laws in the Philippines govern redundancy but offer little guidance on how companies should introduce AI into workplaces or consult employees over its use.
The Philippines' outsourcing sector is also non-unionised, leaving many workers with little formal say over how new technologies are deployed.
The government says that it, and the private sector have a responsibility to retrain workers, and risks falling behind competitors like India and Singapore.
"To be completely honest, I think we're slightly behind. We have to catch up," says Leandro Aguirre of the Philippines Department of Information and Communications Technology.
"We have to double our efforts to put our people in a position where they will not be displaced but actually thrive in this growing AI race."
The government has committed to upskilling more than 300,000 outsourcing workers, but Aguirre acknowledges that the Philippines may need to rethink the economic model that helped make it an outsourcing centre.
"We relied heavily on foreign direct investment," he says. "But I think we also need to focus on local talent and local companies."
The ambition, he says, is to build home-grown AI companies capable of creating higher-value jobs.
Aguirre rejects calls for sweeping new AI legislation, arguing that existing labour, privacy and consumer protection laws can be adapted more quickly through regulatory guidance.
"The benefits of AI have to trickle down to people," he says. "It can't just benefit employers."
For more than 20 years, the Philippines built one of the world's most successful outsourcing industries by selling the skills of its people to multinational companies.
AI may not end that model, but it is certainly changing it, and risks leaving some workers behind.
Additional reporting by Jaltson Akkanath Chummar and Regine Cabato

title: Lucy Davis urges women to check their breasts for cancer - here's how
description: The actress from The Office TV series says her breast lump was tiny and not a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot.
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
Lucy Davis as Dawn in The Office
Signs of breast cancer are not always a lump in the traditional sense, so what should you look for?
Actress Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of the popular TV series The Office, has revealed she has incurable breast cancer .
On Instagram , external , the 53-year-old said it had spread to her bones and it was too late for chemo.
She added: "The initial lump that I felt, wasn't a 'lump' as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny."
Here's how to check yourself at home.
The NHS says to check your breasts , external or chest about once a month.
That helps you learn what looks and feels normal for you, making it easier to notice any abnormal changes.
Breasts can naturally look and feel a bit different at different phases of your menstrual cycle, and change a bit as you age.
Instead, pay attention to:
a lump or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit
a change in the skin of your breast, such as dimpling (it may look like orange peel) or redness, which may be harder to see on black or brown skin
a change in size or shape of one or both breasts, or either side of your chest â?? it's common for breasts to be different sizes, but check for any changes that are not normal for you
nipple discharge (if you're not pregnant or breastfeeding), which may have blood in it
a change in the shape or look of your nipple, such as it turning inwards (inverted nipple) or a rash appearing on it (it may look like eczema)
sores or ulcers on your chest
Look at your breasts or chest in a mirror to look for any changes. Start with your arms by your sides and then raise them up.
Feel around each breast or side of your chest in a circular motion all the way up to your collarbone and under each armpit. Use a mix of light and firmer pressure. Do not press so hard it hurts.
Feel around and over each nipple.
you have a lump or swelling in your breast, chest or armpit
you have any changes in your breasts, chest or nipples that are not normal for you
you have pain in your breast or armpit that does not go away

title: Belfast - 'Unrecognisable city' hosted All-Ireland Fleadh
description: Organisers and participants hail the "transformational" impact of the cultural festival on the city.
author: Eimear Flanagan , Daniel Logan, Emmet McElhatton
content:
Footfall numbers exceeded even the most optimistic expectations with 1.6m visits clocked up during the eight-day festival
For those involved in Belfast's Irish traditional music scene through the 1970s, '80s and '90s, the idea of the Fleadh Cheoil na hÃ?ireann [All-Ireland Fleadh] one day coming to the city was one too ridiculous to even contemplate.
Veteran folk singer Neil Martin said nobody during the Troubles would have "thought it would have been safe".
"It could have been targeted in a way that could have endangered life, you could have been sure of that," he said.
The 2026 festival exceeded expectations, bringing 1.6m visits to the city over eight days of celebrations.
For Martin, the Fleadh showed him how far Belfast has come over the last few decades and also served as a reminder that, even after 60 years of playing music, there are still some surprises left.
Neil Martin was bowled over by the music, atmosphere and togetherness of All Ireland Fleadh
Martin recalled his first All-Ireland Fleadh in Listowel in 1973, but said the prospect of the festival coming north was not a realistic aspiration then.
"It's not something I thought I'd ever see, to be honest," he said.
"But because of the political unrest here and the Troubles, I just couldn't have imagined that it would have been accepted by all sections of the community here."
But Northern Ireland is not the same place it was then.
Much has changed, including, Martin said, the idea that traditional music is "only for Catholics and nationalists".
For this he gives credit to the organisers of Belfast Trad Fest.
Reviewing his experience of the week, he said it was like he was "in a dream walking through the town" and the mood all week was one of joy and "bonhomie".
"People were there for music and to celebrate music, and that's when music comes into its own: when it goes beyond nationality or religion, when it just travels on another plane, and it becomes this international language that we can all appreciate and understand."
He described loving being part of an atmosphere of multiculturalism and global inclusiveness that defined much of the celebrations.
"What I really really enjoyed as well was the microcosm here at home, of the Belfast Bands Forum, for example, accepting the Fleadh and coming into the Fleadh and embracing it.
"I just thought some of that was very, very brave, and very true to what music is."
Belfast native Linda Ervine said seeing how Belfast has changed was emotional
Linda Ervine - an Irish language activist who hails from a unionist background - said she did not recognise her native city during the Fleadh.
A city centre, once so scarred by sectarian violence that it was barricaded off every night, was turned into one big, pedestrianised stage to showcase all its traditions.
"How different things felt this week - just music and joy everywhere really," she told BBC News NI.
"I actually felt very emotional, and I didn't expect that and I think it was because how much Belfast has changed."
Ervine was seven years old when the Troubles began in the late 1960s.
Years of bombings, shootings and arson attacks meant Belfast city centre was locked down every night behind metal security barriers known as the "ring of steel".
Access to parts of Belfast city centre was restricted to day time hours only during the Troubles
During the day, shoppers had to queue up for bag searches - a custom that Ervine grew up believing was the norm.
"I remember my mummy taking us over to her sister's in Liverpool and I think I was probably about 10 or 11 at the time," she recalled.
"When they took us into a shop, the first thing myself and my brother did was we put our arms out to be searched.
"I remember her saying: 'No, no, we don't do that here'," she laughed.
Ervine, whose husband is an ex-leader of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), now works for an organisation which promotes the "shared history" of the Irish language.
She acknowledged that Belfast's security barriers were removed many years ago as a result of the peace process.
But she hopes the cross-community efforts of fleadh organisers and the "carnival atmosphere" they created helps break down cultural barriers that still persist.
"How welcoming it was to hear so much Irish spoken just around the city centre - it was just wonderful," she said.
The Duke of York's Willie Jack, who, along with fellow directors of Commercial Inns Ltd also runs the Harp Bar and the Dark Horse, said the "scenes that we had and experienced over the last eight days were just out of this world".
"It was such a friendly city," Jack said, adding "there was not one incident in any of our establishments that would cause to get anyone involved, not even any bad words, it was just such a positive image of Belfast.
"I've lost my voice, I talked non-stop."
His visitors ranged from Snow Patrol frontman Gary Lightbody to Jimmy Nesbitt and the taoiseach (Irish prime minster).
"The number of people I've had from Cork who didn't know we existed like this and how much Belfast has moved on," he added.
Willie Jack said he has never seen Belfast so vibrant and positive in 40 years
Jack agrees Belfast is now a different place.
"During the Troubles the streets were dark but even then we've had 27 years of peace since the Good Friday Agreement. Never have I seen a city so vibrant and so positive in 40 years," Jack said.
As someone who has been in the industry for more than 40 years, Jack feels it would have been unimaginable 20, 30 years ago and that the city has gone "exponentially upwards".
"It's like a rocket, have we created a monster for next year? Perhaps. It proves the city can cope."
Maurice Brown, director of the Ulster Bands showcase, said his involvement this week was "beyond my wildest dreams".
"To deliver Northern Irish unionist Ulster-Scots marching band culture not only to the Fleadh, but to open it, to close it, have our own event in Titanic slipways, play with the Ulster Orchestra, it's beyond my wildest dreams.
"It genuinely feels like I'm living in a parallel universe.
"Let's keep that buzz going, lets see where this can take us, it's been groundbreaking for everyone."
Brown said the week was the "greatest Belfast has ever had in living memory".
"Every culture has been represented, every tradition. Everybody who has wanted to take part in the Fleadh has been afforded the luxury to do so in a safe and comfortable environment," he said.
Maurice Brown thinks the fleadh was a huge success and a demonstration of how inclusive Belfast has become
Brown praised the inclusiveness of the festival.
"Those that stayed away, that's their choice to stay away, that opinion is absolutely valid, but those that wanted to come in, wanted to get involved have been able to do so."
He said he felt being a unionist should not exclude him from putting his culture on display for the city's natives and visitors.
Brown, a former member of the UK military, said the Fleadh highlighted how much Northern Ireland has changed over the past few decades.
"I'm not afraid to say it but I spent 23 years in Her Majesty's armed forces, and Belfast whenever I left in 1996 was a different place.
"I came home in 2019 to make some sort of difference, more as a father and citizen of the city and here we are seven years later and you just need to look around you, what more could we ask for?"
For Gerry Lennon, the Fleadh was a "watershed moment" for a city he has championed for the past 25 years as chief executive of Visit Belfast.
He added feedback has been overwhelmingly positive with visitors telling his staff: "You should be very proud of your city."
He hopes such reviews will boost tourism from the Republic of Ireland which is a "core" market for his organisation.
The opening ceremony was billed as a "multicultural showcase" and included bagpipes and Highland dancing
But for a city that was once home to the most-bombed hotel in Europe, Belfast was not always the easiest destination to sell.
Lennon acknowledged the "narrative of our city" had already changed significantly since the early days of the peace process, but he added the Fleadh has been "transformational" in dismantling preconceptions about Belfast.
"There's always that 'legacy negativity' sitting there in places and events like this - and this event in particular - has probably just smashed through that."
He attributes the success of the festival to its "totally inclusive" nature and its sole focus on "the celebration of music and culture and dance and song".
"When that is the focus, there's more that we have in common than we have that separates us," he said.
"That's why I think this is a truly milestone event."

title: Artemis II: The 40 minutes when the astronauts lose contact with Earth
description: As the astronauts pass behind the Moon they will experience a moment of silence and solitude as communication with the Earth is blocked.
author: Rebecca Morelle , Alison Francis, Kevin Church
content:
Earth as seen from the Orion capsule in a new image taken last week
No-one will have been further from home than the Artemis astronauts.
But as the Earth shrinks ever smaller in their rear-view mirror, they've had a constant connection with mission control in Houston, Texas. The calm words from the Nasa team have given the crew a comforting link with home.
That link is about to be lost.
As the astronauts pass behind the Moon at about 23:47 BST (18:47 EDT) on Monday, the radio and laser signals that allow the back-and-forth communication between the spacecraft and Earth will be blocked by the Moon itself.
For about 40 minutes, the four astronauts will be alone, each with their own thoughts and feelings, travelling through the darkness of space. A profound moment of solitude and silence.
This video can not be played
'Spectacular!' - Rebecca Morelle reacts to the launch
Artemis pilot Victor Glover told us he hopes the world will use the time to come together.
"When we're behind the Moon, out of contact with everybody, let's take that as an opportunity," he told BBC News before the mission. "Let's pray, hope, send your good thoughts and feelings that we get back in contact with the crew."
More than 50 years ago, the Apollo astronauts also experienced the isolation brought by a loss of signal during their missions to the Moon.
Perhaps none more so than Apollo 11's Michael Collins.
Astronaut Michael Collins said he felt "truly alone" on the far side of the Moon
In 1969, while Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin made history taking the first steps on the lunar surface, Collins was alone in the command module, orbiting the Moon.
As his craft passed behind the far side, contact with the pair on the lunar surface, as well as with mission control, vanished for 48 minutes.
He described the experience in his 1974 memoir Carrying the Fire, saying he felt "truly alone" and "isolated from any known life", but that he did not feel fear or loneliness.
In later interviews, he described the peace and tranquillity brought by the radio silence, saying it offered a break from the constant requests from mission control.
First stop, the Moon. Next stop, Mars? Why Nasa's mission matters
Everything you need to know about Nasa's Artemis II mission
Who are the crew - and what are they taking to the Moon?
Artemis II: Inside the Moon mission to fly humans further than ever
The spectacular new image of Earth taken by the crew
13 Minutes Presents: Artemis II
The BBC's space podcast tells the story of Artemis II- Nasa's mission to loop around the moon.
Back on Earth, the blackout will be a tense time for those with the job of maintaining contact with the spacecraft.
At the Goonhilly Earth Station in Cornwall, in the south-west of England, a huge antenna has been collecting signals from the Orion capsule, carefully pinpointing its position throughout its journey, and feeding this information back to Nasa HQ.
Matt Cosby, Goonhilly's chief technology officer, told the BBC: "This is the first time we're tracking a spacecraft with humans on it.
"We're going to get slightly nervous as it goes behind the Moon, and then we'll be very excited when we see it again, because we know that they're all safe."
But the hope is these dropouts in communications could soon become a thing of the past. And Cosby says that will be essential as Nasa â?? and other space agencies around the world â?? begin to build a Moon base and ramp up further exploration.
"For a sustainable presence on the Moon, you need the full comms - you need the full 24 hours a day, even on the far side, because the far side will want to be explored as well," he said.
Programmes like the European Space Agency's Moonlight are planning to launch a network of satellites around the Moon to provide continuous and reliable communication coverage in the future.
For the Artemis astronauts, their time without contact with the Earth will allow them to devote all of their attention to the Moon.
They'll spend the blackout dedicated to lunar observation â?? taking images, studying the Moon's geology and simply gazing at its splendour.
When they emerge from the Moon's shadow, and that signal is re-established, the world will breathe a collective sigh of relief.
And the history-making astronauts will be able to share their incredible views with everyone back home.

title: Hollywood actor seeks help from Shropshire vicar for documentary
description: Rev Paul Cawthorne helped Michael Sheen identify sites where toxic waste was dumped in the 1970s.
author: David Tooley
content:
Hollywood actor Michael Sheen is pictured with environmental chemist Dr Dave Megson, and the Rev Paul Cawthorne
A Shropshire vicar played a key role in a new two-part BBC documentary featuring Welsh Hollywood actor Michael Sheen's investigation into toxic waste dumps.
The Rev Paul Cawthorne, priest in charge of churches in the Hadnall area, is also a long time environmental campaigner.
He began looking into the history of the former landfill site at Stoney Hill, in Telford, where former chemical giant, Monsanto, is known to have legally dumped waste in the mid to late 1980s.
"When I found out about the Monsanto chemical dumping at Stoney Hill, I next identified Sutton Walls in Herefordshire, then Cefn Mawr in north Wales," he said.
"I then went around south Wales valleys identifying historically documented sites which needed additional testing," he added.
Cawthorne said he has been on a 20 year mission to uncover the truth.
He said that "dangerously elevated levels" of polychlorinated biphenyls - toxic man-made chemicals which don't easily break down in nature - were found in nine out of 10 sites discussed in the Buried BBC radio series.
"The results at some were literally off the scale and will have a big impact in professional circles, assuming they cannot continue to try to ignore them now," he said.
Details of Monsanto's involvement at Stoney Hill between 1985-1988, when it was managed by Shropshire County Council, was revealed in a recent Freedom of Information request.
Cawthorne has now called on the current site owners, Telford and Wrekin Council, to order a full fresh statutory investigation into the former landfill site near Coalbrookdale.
The LDRS asked Telford and Wrekin Council for a response to Cawthorne's repeated calls for an investigation.
A council spokesperson said: "Information about Stoneyhill landfill site's active management plan is available on the council's website."
The council took over the management of the former landfill site in 1998 and states on its website there is "no evidence in the records received from Shropshire County Council that toxic materials or waste were tipped in Stoneyhill landfill."
It also carries out regular testing and it states these have not identified any cause for concern.
The council's website adds that a detailed assessment and review was carried out by the Environment Agency in 2008 and "as a result the site is not considered a harm to the local environment."
For the documentary, he put his focus on the former activities of Monsanto, which produced a range of chemicals at factories in Newport, south Wales, and Ruabon, near Chirk, before the disposal legislation began to tighten in 1974.
Buried with Michael Sheen, comes to BBC Two, BBC One Wales and BBC iPlayer from Monday 17 August.
