title: Calls for public inquiry into Jason Arday media 'witchhunt'
description: Lord Simon Woolley said Arday had been "hounded" by the media and pursued relentlessly.
author: Ruth Comerford
content:
Public figures and friends of Jason Arday have called for a public inquiry into media coverage surrounding the former Cambridge professor before his death.
Labour MP Diane Abbott and actress Jameela Jamil are among 30,000 signatories of a letter to the prime minister, which claims Arday's death followed "two weeks of relentless harassment".
The letter issued by group Good Law Project - which had been representing Arday after he stood down from his Cambridge role amid a plagiarism row - said many of its signatories had warned media outlets about the intensity of their reporting.
Lord Woolley, principal of Homerton College at Cambridge, said Arday had been subjected to a "vicious witch hunt".
Analysis: Jason Arday's death will send shockwaves through a divided academia
Jason Arday death 'tragedy on so many levels' says PM
Jason Arday, ex-Cambridge professor at centre of plagiarism row, found dead
Green Party leader Zack Polanski, and Labour MPs Bell Ribiero-Addy, Clive Lewis and Nadia Whittome are among the politicians to have signed the statement, alongside former England footballer Eni Aluko, National Education Union general secretary Daniel Kebede, and broadcaster Carol Vorderman.
It calls for an "immediate public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press".
Arday, 41, was found dead at an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday. He had resigned as a Cambridge professor of sociology of education on 5 August after allegations of plagiarism and questions about some of his achievements. He had denied the claims.
Liverpool John Moores University - which awarded Arday his PhD in 2015 - concluded that he had not plagiarised work.
The row first erupted after another academic - self-defined "race realist" Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 - said he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor's work. Cofnas's post had been terminated amid a backlash to his view that under a true meritocracy black people would "disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment".
Lord Woolley told BBC Radio 4's Broadcasting House programme on Sunday he and a number of close friends had met Arday four days before he was found dead at a south London address.
He said Abbott and social activist Misan Harriman were among those who gathered to offer support as they had also experienced " horrible media attention ".
He said Arday felt "hounded" and the relentless media coverage had been "a bloodsport".
"Diane said to him, she held his hand, and said we will help you get through this," he added.
"But on that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief."
Lord Woolley said issues of plagiarism were constant in academia and that a number of individuals, who had been accused of plagiarism had not been subjected to the attention Arday had received.
"We have to ask this question, we have to talk about - which a lot of people don't want to talk about, is racism. You have to look at negatively differential treatment."
On 6 August Cambridge announced an independent investigation into Arday's appointment.
A University of Cambridge spokesperson told the BBC that during his time at the university, Arday had received a range of support in relation to his physical and mental well-being, including counselling and support and advice.
"Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation," they added.
Cambridge celebrated Arday's appointment as a young black professor, one of a tiny and visible minority in academia. Only one per cent of professors in UK universities are black, making each appointment hugely significant.
More than Â£90,000 has now been raised for Arday's family, after Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon, who is also among the signatories to the petition, launched a fundraiser.
A vigil organised by group Stand Up To Racism is set to take place on Monday evening in Trafalgar Square.

title: Why Japanese firms are being so slow to use AI
description: Japanese risk aversion and conservatism blamed for slow AI take-up by the country's business sector.
author: Michael Fitzpatrick
content:
Studies show that Japanese firms are dragging their feet when it comes to using AI
Facing acute labour shortages, ageing demographics and chronic productivity problems, Japanese companies should be fertile ground for the take-up of artificial intelligence (AI). Yet, compared with the US and UK, adoption in many workplaces remains sluggish and cautious.
Japan's response to AI is beginning to resemble one of the country's slow-moving, traditional Noh plays.
All the masked characters up on stage agree that action is urgent, and the call is repeated with solemn agreement. Yet the actors remain frozen in place.
Great for heightening drama, terrible for addressing the country's immediate difficulties.
Data showing the use of AI in the workplace suggests that Japan has fallen behind. Just 8.4% of Japanese workers use AI as part of their job, according to a report , external at the end of last year by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD).
By contrast, separate statistics puts the US figure at 50%, , external and the UK at 32%. , external In Singapore, which is said to have seen the second-highest , external take up of AI after the United Arab Emirates, and the most in Asia, 56% of workers are said to use AI "multiple times a week". , external
US and Japan take action to prop up yen in rare joint move
AI used new levels of 'autonomy and deception' to trick people in safety test
So why is Japan dragging its feet? Austin Xu, co-founder of US start-up Kuse AI, says it is due to Japanese companies being conservative and risk adverse. His business recently set up an office in Japan to sell its AI systems to firms in the country.
"There are organisations where process and consensus culture genuinely slow things down," he says. "Where tolerance for AI mistakes is close to zero, especially in anything client facing. Some would rather leave a role unfilled than let a machine handle it."
Xu says the situation in the US is very different, with some businesses already allowing AI agents far more freedom to boost productivity. "In the US, AI colleagues enter as helpers and gradually become part of the workflow. The attitude [of US bosses] is often - let it try, then correct it."
He adds that Japanese companies need more proof before they trust AI enough to use it.
Parrisa Haghirian, professor of international management at the Kyoto University of Advanced Science, agrees that many Japanese companies are too risk adverse to look at AI.
"The challenges of adopting it are the same as adopting any change in Japanese firms. This is why AI use is still quite limited and cautious, especially in the workplace."
Haghirian also contrasts this with the more entrepreneurial culture of the US, arguing that Japanese firms are highly sensitive to error, uncertainty and reputational risk.
"Since generative AI is still not fully reliable, it is mainly used [in Japan] for low-risk tasks such as writing, summarising, or information gathering, but much less for core operations or decision-making and for improving overall processes," she says.
Japanese companies are said to be concerned that AI may make errors
Japan's healthcare sector is said to be particularly slow to look at AI, with some hospitals yet to even fully digitalise patient files. "Paper documents accumulate at a staggering scale," says one employee at a Japanese hospital, who asked not to be named. "It's like the Stone Age."
The Japanese government is aware of the wider problem of low AI adoption, and is trying to get more companies to take up the technology. Last year its AI Promotion Act was passed , external by the country's parliament.
This aims to use light-touch regulation to encourage businesses to invest more in AI. Tokyo pledges that Japan will become "the world's most-friendly country for developing and utilizing AI".
The government believes that the increased use of AI can help Japan improve its productivity. Currently it continues to have the worst level , external in the G7 group of advanced nations.
Japan's Ministry of Finance says that AI adoption by businesses has already increased substantially, , external with 75% of companies now using the technology, up from 11% five years ago.
Japan is said to be facing a shortfall of IT workers
However, critics argue that at each of these businesses only a tiny proportion of staff are actually using the AI, and that those who do so are only using it to a very limited extent.
Prof Yasushi Ogasawara, an expert on Japan's social system and technology at Meiji University, says there aren't enough tech-savvy people in the workforce.
"Although the Japanese like playing with gadgets such as smartphones, digital literacy is low here," he says.
This is highlighted by one report earlier this year which said Japan faced a shortfall , external of almost 800,000 IT professionals by 2030.
Many companies are also said to struggle with out-of-date computer systems, with around 60% more than 20-years-old.
Moreover, Ogasawara adds that Japanese companies are under more pressure to avoid fuelling unemployment than they are to develop AI which could result in job losses.
"The government is talking about AI, re-skilling, digital skills, but in reality, it is difficult to adapt human resources to digital skills because the top priority is to maintain full employment," he says.
But there is a shift in recruitment, with some companies now prioritising "AI literacy" in their new graduate hiring.
In the private sector, larger firms such as Kanematsu, a major general trading company, are hiring savvy graduates such as Uta Yamaguchi who joined in April.
"I use AI quite often at work," she says. "Many of my colleagues use it a lot. For writing emails for my boss, summarising complicated documents, meeting recording and summarising."
But, by contrast with the US, she says AI systems that can autonomously handle multi-step work are still virtually unheard of in Japan.
However, her employer, known for its forward thinking, now has them onboard.
Ogasawara says that "change in Japan is limited". He adds: "Japanese society expects painless reform, so I think it can be said that drastic reform is difficult, to say the least."
Disruption may be a dirty word in Japan, but without it the productivity gains the country needs could remain elusive.

title: Kildare: Multiple dead and four injured following two-vehicle crash
description: The collision occurred on on the M9 Northbound at about 03:00 local time on Sunday in County Kildare.
author: Adam Mandeville
content:
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly described the crash as a "horrific incident"
A number of people have died and four people have been taken to hospital following a two-vehicle crash in County Kildare.
The collision occurred on on the M9 Northbound at Junction 3 at about 03:00 local time on Sunday.
GardaÃ­ (Irish police) said a vehicle had been travelling on the wrong side of the carriageway when a head on collision occurred with a second car. They said there were a "number of fatalities".
The driver and front passenger, both female and aged in their 30s, of the second car have been removed from the scene to Tallaght University Hospital and both remain in critical condition.
A female rear seat passenger, aged in her 20s, was taken to St. Luke's General Hospital and is in a serious condition.
The third passenger, who is a child, has been removed to Children's Health Ireland at Crumlin and is in a serious condition.
The section of the M9 from Junction 3 to Junction 4 northbound and southbound remains closed with local diversions in place.
Irish broadcaster RTÃ? have reported that gardaÃ­ said there was no pursuit taking place when the collision occurred.
GardaÃ­ said FiosrÃº (the Office of the Police Ombudsman) has been notified of the incident.
FiosrÃº's on-call team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.
The watchdog said a FiosrÃº investigation relates to incidents involving contact with gardaÃ­ where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured.
It said a referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaÃ­ have been accused of wrongdoing.
"Instead, it means that FiosrÃº should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaÃ­ may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it added.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly described those injured in the crash as "family members" who were "travelling innocently" when they were struck by the car driving on the wrong side of the motorway.
He described it as a "horrific incident" and "irresponsible and dangerous driving".
"What makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media likes regardless of the potentially devastating impact it might have on innocent people and themselves."
Kelly added that officers "do what they can to stop such vehicles while also taking into consideration all other road users".
"GardaÃ­ are put in a really challenging situation dealing with such incidents."
Sinn FÃ©in TD for Kildare South ShÃ³nagh NÃ­ Raghallaigh described the scenes as "absolutely catastrophic".
"My deepest sympathies go out to the families of those who have lost their lives, and for those who remain in a critical condition in hospital," she said.
"My heart also goes out to the first responders and all of those working in our emergency services who were met with the most horrific of scenes this morning.
"This loss of life is colossal and the effect those losses will have on their friends and families is incalculable," Ms NÃ­ Raghallaigh added.
GardaÃ­ are appealing for any persons who may have witnessed this collision to come forward.
They are also appealing to road users who were travelling on the M9 northbound or southbound between 02:00 and 03:00 on Sunday and who may have dashcam footage of the incident or surrounding area to make this footage available to investigating GardaÃ­.

title: Madhya Pradesh: Happy Indian labourers say '$52,400 diamond' find in Panna to change life
description: The seven men found a 17.96-carat gem-quality diamond in central India's Panna.
author: Geeta Pandey
content:
Akhilesh Pal and six others leased the mine in Panna's Sarokha village for a meagre sum two years back
Seven poor labourers in Panna, a diamond mining area in central India, have made a discovery that they say has the potential to change their lives forever.
The delighted men said they found a large diamond on a plot of land they had leased two years back.
On the weighing scale, the rock measured 17.96 carats and Panna diamond official Ravi Patel said it was "gem quality" - one of the finest varieties of natural diamonds that exist.
Describing the diamond as "precious", Patel said it would be put up for auction in the first half of October. He estimated its worth to be at least 5m rupees ($52,400; Â£38,800).
The diamond weighs 17.96 carats and has been described as a "precious... gem-quality" rock
Diamond finds are not so rare in Panna, which is in Madhya Pradesh state - home to most of India's diamond reserves .
The district is among India's least developed and its residents face poverty, water scarcity and unemployment.
With few job opportunities in the city, residents hope for a prized find to improve their fortunes and the region remains a prime destination for diamond hunters.
But finders are not always keepers.
Reports , external say a majority of Panna's miners are daily-wage labourers who work for lease-holders - if they find a diamond, the money goes to the lease-holder and not the miners themselves.
But the latest find is one of the few cases where the actual finders would benefit.
The mine in Panna's Sarokha village was leased for a meagre sum by Akhilesh Pal and six others two years back, Press Trust of India reported.
Pal said the mine had been shut for a year and was opened only recently. On Monday, as he inspected the mine after heavy rains, he spotted the rock.
"We had been mining there for about two years," he said, "but we had no luck, so we closed the mine for a year. We had started another mine right next to it."
"When we went there to inspect the new one, we also looked inside the old mine, and that's where we found it - right on top," he added.
Patel said the diamond would be put up for sale at the next quarterly auction due in October when buyers from India and abroad would be able to bid for it.
Reports said the government would deduct a 12% royalty from the sale proceeds and the remaining money would be divided equally among the seven workers.
For some of the poor labourers, the find is set to change the course of their lives - local media reports quoted three of them as saying they were too poor to get married so far and this windfall would now help them find brides.

title: Grant Shapps blocked from standing again for the Conservatives
description: Kemi Badenoch tells the BBC she leads a "new party full of new people" as ex-MP is rejected as a candidate.
author: Chris Mason
content:
This video can not be played
Watch: Badenoch questioned on Grant Shapps in full
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the BBC she leads "a brand new party full of new people" - after it emerged in the Spectator , external that the former cabinet minister and Tory party chairman Sir Grant Shapps has been rejected as a Conservative Party parliamentary candidate.
Sir Grant, who has declined to comment, served in nine ministerial roles in government as well as co-chairing the party.
In cabinet, he served as home secretary, defence secretary, transport secretary, business secretary, energy secretary and net zero secretary.
He was also a Foreign Office Minister, housing minister and international development minister , external .
He lost his Welwyn Hatfield seat to Labour's Andrew Lewin in 2024 by 3,799 votes after representing it since 2005.
But his application to stand again for the Conservatives at the next general election has been declined.
One party source told the BBC "it reflects badly on Kemi's temperament. North Korean purges don't work in British politics".
Badenoch told a news conference in central London: "We don't treat our former MPs or our candidates like tittle-tattle for Westminster gossip.
"What I will say is that we're going to be announcing candidates shortly, and you will see that this is a very different party from the one that was removed from government in 2024."
Grant Shapps served in nine different ministerial roles
Asked repeatedly about her decision, Badenoch said that "commenting on individual applications would be absolutely wrong" but added that "I want people to know that this is a new Conservative party.
"It is not going to be making the mistakes of the past. We lost 250 MPs at the last election.
"We are changing policies, we are changing people, we are changing process. What I have said is we want people who are going to meet the standards which we are setting. Who are going to abide by the policies I have put red lines on. There could be all sorts of reasons for any individual to be allowed or not allowed on the list."
Badenoch has insisted that future Conservative candidates must agree to abandoning net zero carbon policies and to withdrawing from the European Convention on Human Rights.
It is not thought Sir Grant would disagree with either of these stances.
He also happens to be the co-chair of Conservatives Together , external , a group founded "to support and represent Conservative candidates."
He received a knighthood in Rishi Sunak's resignation honours list for "political and public service."

title: What time and where might you see the solar eclipse in Scotland
description: Hopes of catching the best view are fading in parts of Scotland as clouds threaten to hide the celestial event.
author: Claire Thomson
content:
This video can not be played
Are people in Scotland in a good position to see the eclipse? Look at our latest forecast to find out
People in Scotland could get the best view of a solar eclipse in nearly three decades on Wednesday - although hopes of a clear sighting are fading in some parts of the country.
Up to 95% of the Sun will slowly disappear behind the Moon in the most dramatic eclipse visible from the UK since August 1999 .
But clouds in some areas are threatening to obscure the celestial event, which is set to last about two hours.
Here is what you need to know about the partial solar eclipse, including the best places to watch it in Scotland and how to do so safely. It is important to never look directly at the Sun.
The solar eclipse peaks in Scotland just after 19:05
Millions anticipate once-in-a-generation solar eclipse - follow live
August 1999 - Eclipse lightens Scotland's day
Astronomers say the best place to see the eclipse is an elevated location with unobstructed views to the west.
Astronomer Royal for Scotland Prof Catherine Heymans said: "People in England are worried about having to find a clear view of the western horizon.
"But that is less of a problem for us in Scotland because the Sun sets later."
That means in general the Sun should be higher in the sky in Scotland at the time of the eclipse, and people will be able to see the event more clearly.
And by the time the Sun sets after approximately 21:00, the event will be well and truly over.
According to Heymans, the Moon will start to move in front of the Sun between about 18:01 and 18:10 BST.
The peak of the eclipse will occur about an hour later, with the whole event ending just before 20:00.
"It is so slow moving. So if you go out and the Sun is not there you have time to walk down the street to a park or climb up a hill," she added.
"The most important thing is to watch the Met Office cloud cover forecast and plan accordingly from there."
What you need to know about Scotland's partial solar eclipse
BBC Weather presenter Joy Dunlop says conditions for viewing the partial solar eclipse will vary across Scotland.
"Southern Scotland is likely to have the most optimal conditions for catching a glimpse of the eclipse as it will be dry with largely clear skies," she said.
"Clearer spells could possibly develop across the central belt and in parts of eastern Scotland.
"But the north west Highlands, Western and Northern Isles will remain cloudy with spells of rain giving very limited or no visibility."
High level cloud could make views hazy across the country.
Whitelee Windfarm Visitor Centre at Eaglesham in East Renfrewshire is hosting one of the biggest eclipse events - but has warned that the weather is "not looking great".
In a Facebook post, it said it could not guarantee a view of the eclipse. Refunds are available for those who have booked but no longer want to attend.
"Cloud cover is predicted and unfortunately you might not be able to see it," it said.
Members of the Galloway Forest Astronomical Society set up equipment ahead of the solar eclipse in 2015
There are a number of community events , external happening across Scotland to mark the occasion:
Beirhope Farm, Hownam, Scottish Borders. The event starts at 17:30 and features a talk from the resident astronomy expert, who will introduce Beirhope's new telescope.
Dirleton Solar Walk, East Lothian. Certified eclipse glasses will be available as part of a "relaxed evening".
Edinburgh Playfair Observatory, Calton Hill, Edinburgh. Members of the Astronomical Society of Edinburgh will be on hand to explain more about the eclipse.
Red Burn Farm, Blantyre, South Lanarkshire. Starting at 18:00, eclipse glasses will be available at the family-friendly event.
Whitelee Windfarm Visitor Centre, Eaglesham, East Renfrewshire. A range of activities are on offer, including space-themed arts and crafts and an adult workshop exploring solar eclipses and the night sky.
Dark Space Planetarium, Kirkcudbright, Dumfries and Galloway. If skies are clear, the Dark Space team will go to the harbour with their solar telescope.
Westport Beach Car Park, Campbeltown, Argyll and Bute. Members of the Kintyre and Gigha Night Sky Group will answer questions and eclipse glasses will be available.
Gigha Village Hall, Argyll and Bute. Meet at Gigha Village Hall at 17:30 before walking up to the viewing location.
Broughty Castle, Dundee. The museum will open for a special public viewing.
Glen Tanar Visitor Centre, Aboyne, Aberdeenshire. Booking is essential to join the team at Glen Tanar for the rare astronomical event.
Tomintoul Skyhide Stargazing Pavillion, Ballindalloch, Aberdeenshire. Both solar telescopes and eclipse glasses will be available.
Masstowie Primary School, Elgin, Moray. Eclipse glasses will be available with SIGMA Moray's Astronomy Club teaching families to watch safely.
Jim Savage-Lowden Observatory, Culloden Moor, Highlands. Visitors are encouraged to stay after the partial solar eclipse to watch the Perseids meteor shower.
Midhowe Broch Car Park, Rousay, Orkney. Astronomers will be on hand to help visitors observe the eclipse safely.
Rum Bunkhouse, Isle of Rum, Highlands. Solar telescopes will be set up at the island's campsite from 18:00.
It is important to never look directly at the Sun and follow proper guidance for safely viewing the eclipse.
Eclipse glasses - which will be handed out at events across Scotland hosted by astronomical societies or bought online - can offer protection from harmful rays of sunlight.
Legitimate pairs will have safety certification ISO 12312-2 or ISO 12312-2:2015 printed somewhere on the glasses, according the Royal Observatory Greenwich.
Regular sunglasses do not provide adequate protection.
"Even if you don't feel like it is painful to look at the Sun, it is still really damaging to the retina," Heymans said.
"It is a two-hour extravaganza as the Moon slowly covers the Sun and then moves away again so it is not just one glimpse, and it is really dangerous to keep looking."
She added that there was a temptation to look at the Sun through the cloud but even that could harm the eyes.
Following the 1999 total solar eclipse, the Royal College of Ophthalmologists reported about 70 cases of people experiencing vision problems after watching the eclipse.
The college said about 40% of those people had looked at it for less than a minute.
Eclipse glasses were given to pupils outside the Glasgow Science Centre in 2015 and can offer protection from the Sun
Alternative methods for safely viewing the eclipse, include using a solar telescope or making a pinhole projector.
"The next best thing is a colander," Heymans said - or any household object with small holes.
The holes in the colander project an indirect image of the Sun on a surface, such as a wall or the ground.
"Normally the sunlight shines through the holes but during the eclipse, chunks will be eaten out of the Sun, and at the peak, it will just be the arc in the shadow of the colander," she explained.
People should also be careful when photographing the eclipse as the Sun can damage the camera on a phone the same way as it can damage the eyes.
Cameras can be protected with eclipse glasses.
The holes in the colander project an indirect image of the Sun on a surface
Parts of Spain and Portugal will witness the phenomenon of a total eclipse on Wednesday but Heymans said Scotland would be "agonisingly close".
The path of the eclipse shadow means the UK will not see a total eclipse, but in Scotland, up to 95% of the Sun will be obscured.
"Solar eclipses happen every couple of years but a total eclipse is very rare and we are a stone's throw away from it," Heymans said.
"Over the course of two hours, the Moon will be biting chunks out of the Sun as it moves across in front of it, blocking the light out."
However, the Sun will not be entirely covered.
The progression of a solar eclipse
While there will be smaller solar eclipses over the next few years, the next total eclipse is not expected to take place until 23 September 2090.
"It will be darker and it will feel a little eerie but we're not going to have the sky go completely dark," she said.
At its peak - weather permitting - only an arc of the Sun will be seen.
"It's going to be agonisingly, frustratingly close but if anyone wants to see a full total eclipse, they will have to leave the UK," Heymans added.

title: Vultures are disappearing in Nigeria - but the 'vulture king' and others are fighting back
description: Some see them as sinister or hunt them for ritual use but these birds play a vital role in nature's cycle.
author: Makuochi Okafor
content:
Some see them as sinister but these birds play a vital role in nature's cycle
"People fear the environment where the shrine is. No evil will ever happen here. So, nobody fights vultures that perch here," a man they call the Vulture King tells the BBC.
Mostly associated with death and decay, perhaps it is not surprising that when vultures disappeared from the skies across many West African cities, they were not missed.
Yet across the continent, their disappearance is becoming impossible to ignore, as conservationists warn that hunting linked to traditional beliefs and spiritual practices continues to threaten several vulture species to the point of near extinction.
Without vultures, ecosystems would lose a natural defence against the spread of disease.
Thankfully in one part of south-eastern Nigeria, residents are bucking the trend.
Awka-Etiti is home to a sacred forest surrounding a shrine dedicated to a deity known as Nguma.
At first glance, the site is an unremarkable cluster of tall trees wrapped in thick greenery. But at its heart stands an ancient tree that locals say has watched over the community for hundreds of years, and remains the spiritual home of the shrine.
This is a largely Christian community but some residents continue to observe traditional practices, in which vultures play a key role.
Local resident Chukwuemeka Igwe, who has earned the nickname King of Vulture, thanks to his tireless volunteer work with Nigeria Conservation Foundation (NCF), says "the indigenous don't hunt vultures".
Instead, locals sometimes offer fresh animal sacrifices at the shrine which attract the birds, he explains.
"And there is an adage we use here that says: 'When you put down a sacrifice and you do not see vulture[s], know that something happened in the spirit world'."
It means that vultures are a good omen when a sacrifice has been made because their presence suggests that the deity has accepted the sacrifice and heard the residents' appeal to its power.
Chukwuemeka Igwe is proud of the nickname given to him
Now in his 50s, Igwe says the birds have been a feature of daily life in this town for as long as he can remember, walking around among humans and scavenging for food.
Yet for many who venture into the wild elsewhere on the continent, vultures are not the first birds to capture their attention. Rarely do we stop to admire vultures through binoculars or photograph in awe.
In the eyes of many people, vultures are downright ugly. But scientists say they provide one of nature's most important cleaning services.
Vultures consume dead animals within hours, helping prevent carcasses from becoming breeding grounds for dangerous bacteria and diseases.
Their disappearance can have serious consequences, says NCF conservation biologist Stella Egbe: "In places where the total collapse of vultures has happened, there has been impact of rising zoonotic diseases."
Vultures' powerful stomach acids allow them to safely consume infected animals, helping stop diseases such as anthrax and rabies from spreading.
Without vultures, experts warn ecosystems lose a natural defence system.
Rapid urban growth across Africa has also played its part, transforming landscapes, and destroying many of the tall trees that the birds nest in.
Cape Vultures are one seven types facing extinction
Habitat loss is far from the only factor.
Poisoning is the cause of death for an estimated 60% of vultures in Africa, according to BirdLife International , external .
These issues will be high on the agenda when researchers from across the region meet in Abuja later this year to review the West African Vulture Conservation Action Plan, which was drafted in 2022.
Experts say the use of vultures and their body parts in traditional medicine and Vodun (also known as Voodoo) has emerged as one of the most significant drivers of their decline, especially in West and southern Africa.
Dead adult vultures in Nigeria used to sell for around 25,000 to 30,000 naira ($18 to $22; Â£13 to Â£16) each - but can now fetch up to 200,000 naira ($145; Â£107) per bird, says Egbe.
Vulture eggs and nests are increasingly targeted too, which for such a slow-breeding species is a catastrophic and "shocking" development, says Egbe.
Adult vultures usually reach sexual maturity between the ages of five and seven, and produce only one chick every year or two. Plus many young vultures do not survive their first year.
"And so you imagine what will happen if a nest is removed and eggs are removed. That means a pair of vultures will not have a next generation for that year. So in addition to hunting, you're removing their habitat, you're removing their homes," she adds.
Seven species of vultures in Africa are now classified as globally Endangered or Critically Endangered by BirdLife International, the authority for birds on the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List.
A recent BirdLife report says African vulture populations have fallen by between 80% and 97% over a period of 50 years.
The group also says that in January 2020 more than 2,000 hooded vultures were found dead in Guinea-Bissau, many with their heads removed - a sign of belief-based practices rather than natural causes, researchers say.
As vulture populations continue to fall across the region, conservationists have been searching for communities where these birds are not hunted, feared or exploited.
They found one such example in Awka-Etiti.
Yet in recent years, Igwe says he and other residents became worried when they noticed outsiders arriving to hunt the birds and vulture numbers dwindled.
In his quest to save the birds he visits markets, buses and public spaces to spread the word: "I tell them that vulture is helpful to human life".
He says he "cannot run away" from his unusual nickname of Ezeudene, or the King of Vulture.
"I'm fighting to make nature exist the way it's supposed to be."
Working with the NCF for the past six years, Igwe has mobilised community leaders, local groups and security teams to protect the birds from outside hunters, with local bylaws now helping to formalise their protection.
Local volunteers monitoring the birds say they have now recorded more than 160 vultures, up from about 20 recorded in 2017.
Nigeria has become a major hub for the illegal trade of vultures, conservationists say, partly because of its biodiversity and porous borders.
"We are doing everything possible to make sure that the smuggling of items, including vultures, including donkeys, and other species outside the country is suppressed to the barest minimum," insists Abdullahi Maiwada, a spokesman for the Nigerian Customs Service.
He says customs officials have carried out seizures of protected wildlife and supported prosecutions linked to illegal trafficking.
It is an example of how Nigeria is trying to live up its commitments as a member of the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (Cites) - under which endangered species are not allowed to be traded across borders.
But Maiwada admits to the BBC that enforcement alone is not enough - education will be crucial too.
"We may not be able to do it without the cooperation or understanding of members of the community," he continues. "If people understand why these species should be preserved, then our enforcement will only be complementary to those who decide to be recalcitrant."
That message has been at the heart of conservation work in Awka-Etiti and across parts of Nigeria.
Although reliable population data remains limited, conservationists say there are encouraging signs in Awka-Etiti, with local engagement helping residents become vigilant against outside hunters.
"The missing vultures are almost back. If you go to the marketplace now, you see vultures. At one time they disappeared, but now they are coming back," Igwe confirms.
Egbe believes that this small, south-eastern town demonstrates what is possible when communities lead conservation efforts.
"What we've done in Awka-Etiti is one very good example of a success story where people have taken charge of what's going on in their environment. That makes us happy."
For Igwe, every returning bird represents hope.
But with populations still collapsing across Africa, he knows protecting them will require much more than one community.

title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
description: Hot weather and the men's football World Cup boosted the economy but the Iran war may weigh on growth
author: Lucy Hooker
content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.
The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.
The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.
Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.
The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.
Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.
The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.
The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.
June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.
Fergus Jimenez-England, associate economist National Institute of Economic and Social Research said the UK economy had "weathered the recent energy shock better than many feared".
Matt Harwood, director of Clarity Plastics, a plastic injection moulding company with sites in Birmingham and Telford, said that while the conflict had affected costs for things like raw materials, there had since been some stabilisation.
"When the Iran war started, availability went down and prices went up," he said. "However, we're seeing that kind of level out now, and prices coming back to the kind of the normal levels again.
"We've tried to stay resilient by carrying on investing. We're now installing a large 1500-ton machine... that's kind of giving us a competitive edge now as well."
But Jimenez-England said the recent pace of growth for the UK economy was unlikely to be sustained.
"Both inflation and unemployment are set to rise in the coming months while business sentiment remains fragile and could dampen further with ongoing energy price volatility.
"The economy has shown welcome resilience so far, but we are not out of the woods yet."
On Wednesday, it emerged that Prime Minister Andy Burnham has been warned by the Treasury that the UK economy may grow by just by 0.9% this year and could be as low as 0.3% in 2027 if disruption in the Strait of Hormuz continues .
Clarity Plastics' Matt Harwood says price volatility caused by the war has calmed
Suren Thiru, chief economist at the Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales, said that while households and firms had "largely shrugged off the shockwaves from the Iran war" much of the growth in the second quarter had been driven by "temporary factors".
This was likely to be followed by a "more painful deceleration" in the next few months, he said, and would make Chancellor John Healey's first Budget in October "more challenging".
Responding to the latest growth figures Healey said: "I know people are worried about the impact of the conflict in the Middle East on their cost of living, which has been too high for too long and it has added pressure on British businesses."
He said the government's aim was to make the country "more resilient" and to "drive growth in every postcode".
Shadow chancellor Sir Mel Stride said Labour had "mismanaged the economy with their tax and borrowing spree, leaving it weak and vulnerable to the effects of shocks like the Iran War.
"Labour need to realise that it's their poor decisions which have stifled growth and made the cost of living worse," he said.
Liberal Democrat Treasury Spokesperson Daisy Cooper MP said the figures were "little to celebrate".
"After Labour's two anti-growth budgets, Burnham needs to urgently get a grip on the economy and get Britain growing again, supercharging economic growth through a new trade deal with the EU, including joining the Single Market," she said.

title: Wakefield dog bite victim dies and police open murder inquiry
description: Police appeal for two people who stopped to help the victim in Wakefield to come forward.
author: Andrew Barton
content:
The incident took place on a disused railway line in Calder Grove, Wakefield
A murder inquiry has begun after the death of a man who was bitten by a dog on a footpath in West Yorkshire.
The 55-year-old was injured in an altercation on a disused railway line off Blacker Lane in Calder Grove, Wakefield, at about 13:30 BST on Saturday. He was taken to hospital in a critical condition but died just after 19:00.
West Yorkshire Police has appealed for two people, one of whom is called Sophie, who stopped to help the injured man to come forward.
A force spokesperson said a 55-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of murder and of being the owner of a dog dangerously out of control in a public place, causing injury. He remains in custody.
Police said a German Shepherd dog believed to have been involved in the incident has been seized by officers.
Det Ch Insp Michael Cox said: "Sadly, a man has died and it is really important that we understand the circumstances of what has taken place.
"We know that two people, one named Sophie, stopped to assist the injured man and direct officers."
He added: "We would urge these two people to come forward to help us with our ongoing inquiries into this tragic incident.
"The initial altercation happened in an area used by walkers and we are urging anyone who has seen or heard any part of the exchange between these two men to please make contact."

title: Full body MOTs - the future of healthcare or a headache for the NHS?
description: The private body scan industry is booming, but is it doing more harm than good?
author: Ruth Clegg
content:
More than 2,000 images were taken of Ruth's skin
I don't mind having my photo taken - triple checked and filtered for Instagram - but 70 cameras pointing at me while I'm down to my knickers is a bit daunting.
A robotic voice tells me to stay still and close my eyes as I stand in a huge curved scanner while classical music plays in the background.
With a flash of light, 2,000 photographs are taken of my body, in the hope of capturing every mark, freckle and mole to analyse for different skin cancers.
This full-body scan is happening at a sci-fi-style clinic in Manchester city centre, with me wearing a dressing gown and hexagon-shaped rubber slippers. The millions of data points collected will create a 3D avatar of my body using AI.
Over the past two years, the market for health MOTs has boomed, with people willing to pay hundreds, or even thousands, for them, and companies such as Prenuvo, Ezra and Neko Health raising millions in venture capital.
While Prenuvo and Ezra offer a whole-body MRI scan, I've opted for Neko Health, which doesn't delve quite as deeply, and comes with a more modest Â£299 price tag. There are currently 100,000 people on its waiting list.
The body scan industry sees this kind of treatment as a new frontier in healthcare
I will be screened for a range of different conditions, including skin cancer, cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, eye conditions like glaucoma, as well as kidney and blood disorders.
I don't have any symptoms, but what if they do find something? More on that later.
The body scan industry sees itself as a new frontier in healthcare, preventing disease before it has a chance to fully appear. But there is scepticism about how beneficial these scans really are for otherwise healthy patients.
My socials are inundated with videos of enthusiastic clients filming themselves in scan machines, getting their bloods taken and testing their grip strength.
Hjalmar Nilsonne, one of the founders of Neko Health, wants to see this preventative treatment available for every individual, not just those who can afford to pay for it.
"While medicine has progressed so much over the past century, primary care is still very basic. Why wait until we see symptoms?" Nilsonne says. "The data is super clear - prevention is preferable to cure."
However, GPs and doctors in the wider NHS are more sceptical, with NHS England warning that the popularity of these scans is leading to more "over-diagnosis, unnecessary investigations and avoidable anxiety".
As well as having a scan myself, I've spoken to two women who had very different experiences.
Annabel had four cancerous markings removed
Annabel Mason-Thompson went for a Neko Health scan in September last year, knowing she had a suspicious-looking mark on her back - but it wasn't flagged by the technology.
"I felt a bit let down if I'm honest," the 50-year-old says. "Their AI scanner failed to pick up any of my four cancerous lesions.
"It was only when I went into the doctor's room after the scan and I pointed out my red mark did they take a look at it."
Further examination confirmed the mark was suspicious, so Neko Health contacted Annabel to say she would need treatment and wrote a letter to her private dermatologist to say the "lesion requires evaluation with a view to possible excision".
Her dermatologist found three more cancerous marks which needed urgent treatment.
"Luckily," she says, "they were all slow-growing basal cell carcinomas. I had to have two cut out and two taken off via cryotherapy."
Neko Health says "member safety and clinical excellence are at the heart of everything" it does. The company said its clinical team did identify a "lesion of concern" and it was reviewed by two of its dermatologists before a referral was made for potential treatment.
"We know that no one system is foolproof," Nilsonne says, "which is why we have multiple lenses - it is crucial that the technology and human expertise work together."
His company's latest data shows that of the 4,362 scans carried out on clients who visited Neko Health's Stockholm headquarters last year, 1.2% discovered life-threatening conditions such as melanoma and leukaemia. A further 4% spotted significant health conditions that required further treatment, and 1.2% flagged conditions that could be reversed such as pre-diabetic blood sugar levels.
While the figures are not representative of the population and only account for those who can afford to pay for this kind of preventive healthcare, Nilsonne says this is an indicator of how medicine should look in the future.
But GPs disagree. Prof Victoria Tzortziou Brown, president of the Royal College of GPs (RCGP), says they haven't seen "convincing evidence" private broad screening tests "improve health outcomes".
She says the results from these private scans can also place an additional strain on the NHS as clients come back for further tests and potential treatment, even "where the findings prove to be clinically insignificant".
Mehvish's long-term blood sugar levels came back very high and she was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes
Mehvish says nothing could have prepared her for what she was told after her full body scan. She left Birmingham's Neko Health clinic with a life-changing diagnosis.
"I expected to feel relief," the 33-year-old says. "Instead, I was told that I had a rare form of diabetes."
After her long-term blood sugar levels came back very high, she had another blood test which confirmed she had suspected diabetes.
She was referred back to her GP, who sent her for an urgent hospital appointment the same day, and was diagnosed with Latent Autoimmune Diabetes in Adults (LADA), a type of diabetes which bridges both type 1 and type 2.
Like type 1, it is an autoimmune condition that attacks the body's pancreatic cells, but it also shares traits with type 2 because it can progress slowly and, depending on the stage of the condition, it can initially be managed with diet and exercise.
"I didn't have any of the symptoms," Mehvish says, "It was difficult to get my head round it - how could I have this condition and not know about it?"
But she says the early, unexpected intervention "saved my life".
Now she injects insulin twice a day, monitors what she eats, and despite missing the spontaneity of her old life, is learning to adapt to her new one.
"I feel so much better, more clarity, less brain fog and I feel so much more balanced."
After my own scan, I'm feeling slightly out of balance. I've been told I have 3,311 skin markings - compared to the average Neko Health client's 845. Three need extra review by the company's dermatologist in Sweden.
"But I don't have any big moles or markings," I say during the post-scan consultation with a doctor. It's my freckles, I'm told, and having freckles puts me at higher risk of skin cancer.
One of the moles that were flagged as needing extra scrutiny by dermatologists in Sweden
Having felt confident I would get a clean bill of health - especially when it comes to my skin - I was a bit unnerved to discover that I'd need to have extra tests.
As well as the three suspicious-looking moles that needed further attention, I also discovered I have an unusual heart rate. The trace from the electrocardiogram (ECG) highlighted an extra wave, known as a bifid P wave, which was referred to Neko Health's in-house cardiologist for review. Thankfully, it came back all clear.
A few days later, I received a follow-up text to say there were no abnormal skin changes that required treatment.
I am one of thousands of clients who has had something flagged as a potential issue, then later found no further treatment was required. Some doctors say this causes unnecessary anxiety and that patients should only rely on national screening programmes through the NHS.
Dr Stephen Harden, president of the Royal College of Radiologists, points to the technology used in the NHS, which targets "specific areas" like the breasts, bowel or cervix, and which he says may be more reliable than a whole-body scan.
But former health minister Steve Brine, who acts as an advisor to a preventative healthcare company, says precautionary scans like the one I had "fit the direction of travel of how people are approaching their health".
"Change is afoot across the NHS - prevention is a huge policy area," Brine says. "We want to identify people's problems before they become patients, so these scans could well become a part of our future healthcare and primary care needs to adapt."
As for me? I was told my heart age was four years younger than my actual age, and on the whole, I was in tip-top health. But I've also learned a valuable lesson - that I could be more at risk of skin cancer because of my freckles.
So, thanks to my time in the scanner, I am now far more enthusiastic about lathering sunscreen all over my body - rather than only on my face.

title: Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding
description: Ofwat has given provisional approval for 13 water companies to charge customers more to pay for investments.
author: Lucy Hooker
content:
Water companies have been given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra Â£3.4bn in coming years to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.
Nearly a third of the extra funding provisionally approved for 13 water companies in England and Wales is earmarked for making sure water services are maintained.
Some of the rest will be used to meet rising demand from housebuilding and data centres and to address pollutants known as "forever chemicals".
Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the proposal was "real money out of family budgets at a time when they are struggling with the cost of living", and an environmental group described the decision as "an insult".
Customers of five water companies - Severn Trent Water, Southern Water, Thames Water, Wessex Water, and South East Water - are facing additional bill rises over the next two years, on top of increases that were already announced in 2024.
The new increases will vary between firms.
Southern, for example, will charge Â£43 extra next year, while South Eastern will only charge Â£1 more in 2029. The increases will only come into effect if they are given final approval later this year.
The other eight water firms identified - Anglian Water, Dwr Cymru Welsh Water, Hafren Dyfrdwy, Northumbrian Water, Wouth West Water, United Utiliites, Yorkshire Water, SES Water - would recover their additional spending through customer bills after 2030.
Many consumers are angry at being asked to pay anything more against a backdrop of interruptions to supply sometimes lasting for days, and rivers, lakes and beaches too polluted to use safely.
But water companies argue that these problems can only be solved by boosting spending to replace pipes, build treatment plants and establish new reservoirs.
Climate change has also increased pressure on the water infrastructure by making heavy rains and heatwaves more frequent.
The regulator, Ofwat, said the extra spending would enable the firms to support growth and better environmental outcomes, and ensure important upgrades were not delayed.
"We will track performance to ensure companies are delivering the expected improvements for customers and the environment," said Helen Campbell, executive director for delivery at Ofwat.
"If they don't, expenditure can be clawed back."
Water companies need approval from the regulator, Ofwat, to raise customers' bills, a process that takes place every five years to set spending budgets for the years ahead.
This decision to allow increased charges comes on top of already-agreed bill rises that were negotiated with the water companies in 2024.
The process allows firms to apply for additional funds for projects that were not known about at the time of the last review.
As part of the outlined increase, Ofwat has approved funding for schemes including provision for new data centres in Manchester, additional wastewater capacity in Newquay and to bring forward work by Wessex Water to tackle PFAS pollutants, originally planned for 2030-35.
However, the decision is provisional. There is a period of public consultation, with a final decision due in December.
Ofwat said water companies had submitted a total of Â£4.3bn worth of requests, but some of their proposed extra spending had been rejected.
Burnham said he understood why people were angry as they had been asked to pay more for years while pollution incidents and leaks continued.
"Where water companies seek to pass unnecessary costs onto households, they will be challenged," he said.
Amy Fairman, from campaign group River Action, said: "Ofwat waving through yet more water bill hikes is an insult."
Water companies had failed to make sufficient investment over the last 30 years, she said, leaving customers with "leaks, pollution and soaring bills".
There should be greater public control of water companies, she added. "No more blank cheques for failure."
Kierra Box, water campaigner at Friends of the Earth said: "Our rivers and seas are chock full of filthy sewage and chemicals, which have seen next to no improvement despite recent bill hikes.
"Now ordinary people are being asked to foot the bill once again to pay for decades of water company inaction on upgrading our crumbling water infrastructure. It's daylight robbery."

title: 'You could smell someone' who worked at Raleigh
description: The company was more than just a employer. For years, it was part of the fabric of Nottingham.
author: Greig Watson
content:
At its height, Raleigh employed 8,000 people and produced thousands of bikes a month
The news the company that owns Raleigh has begun insolvency proceedings means one of Nottingham's most prestigious manufacturing names may have reached the end of its journey.
From being one of the city's big three employers - along with Boots and Players cigarettes - with 8,000 staff, it may have finished its days being little more than a logo.
But during the decades of its existence, it touched the lives of countless people, both those who worked there and those who enjoyed its bicycles.
Some of those tell their stories about what Raleigh meant to them.
For decades Raleigh exported its bicycles across the world, including this shop in Paris
Mark Hallam grew up being able to see the Raleigh factory from his backyard.
He said: "Raleigh - Players and Boots too - came to the school offering careers and since it was so close I went for Raleigh.
"I started in 1978, starting with how to build brakes and put spokes in wheels.
"It had such a great atmosphere, though you had to be able to take having the mickey taken out of you!
"It was diverse and so friendly, so full of characters, the social club was a great place."
Notorious Nottinghamshire on Raleigh
"One weird thing was you could smell if someone worked for Raleigh. I think it was the metal mixed with grease and oil.
"And the factory dominating the area. I once walked past the gate just before four o'clock and everyone was pressed up against it, ready to run.
"People would say, 'get the bus before Raleigh chucks out'.
"But here's the thing, I never rode a Raleigh as I couldn't afford one," he said.
David Marsland (pictured centre) was present for a visit by Princess Diana in 1990
David Marsland reluctantly followed his father into the company.
He said: "I wanted to be a surveyor but couldn't get a job.
"I had grown up with Raleigh and joined in 1973, and I gained new friends at every stage of my 47 years and met my wife there, so it was very much the background to my life.
"There used to be so many people working there we not only had a football team, we had our own league.
"But then the redundancies started coming - I don't know how many times I walked into an office not knowing whether I would have a job when I came out.
"One time we had all these plans for a new factory in Bulwell but when it became clear that our steel bicycles couldn't match the prices of aluminium bicycles from the Far East, it all got binned.
"I think that was the moment Raleigh changed."
Some staff covered the distances inside the factory by riding bikes
Sarah Nixon, from Daybrook in Nottinghamshire, said her parents met at the company.
She said: "My mum worked in the offices and my dad was a work study engineer, this was in the 1950s.
"They described it as a really great place to work, it was very social, more of a community than a workplace.
"The other thing they would talk about was the size of the place, which is something I don't think we appreciate these days.
"My dad told me they used to ride bikes between the departments because it was just that huge."
The 1960 movie Saturday Night and Sunday Morning featured a lead character who worked at the factory
For Maureen Vines, Raleigh was also a family affair.
"We lived near Faraday Road, opposite the White Horse pub," she said.
"Most of my uncles worked at Raleigh, my aunts worked at Players, but I remember the road being full of people on bikes.
"When they filmed Saturday Night and Sunday Morning - the main chap in that works at Raleigh - they filmed it in the road outside.
"One of my uncles, Charlie, he rode his bike for that and you can still see him in the background, in the film, riding down the street.
"It's one of the firms which built Nottingham."
Some Raleigh bicycles lasted for decades, being used to carry several generations
Helen Crowder's family is linked with Raleigh in a slightly different way.
"We lived in Grantham in the 50s and I was promised a Raleigh bicycle if I passed my 11+ [the exam to get into grammar school]," she said.
"Luckily I did that and my parents said, 'right, we'll have to go to Nottingham' which was quite an adventure because we had to get the train.
"But I had that bike for a long, long time.
"I was tall, so I got a full-sized bike and I used it through school and my teens and used it when I started work.
"I moved away when I married and I left it with my mother, but when we came back I got it again and rode with each of my three children in turn on the back.
"It was a super-strong, well-made bike, really excellent and I only had to give it up when it was really worn out.
"I must have ridden it for the best part of 50 years."
Even in the 1980s, Raleighs were still a popular choice for children
Andrew Dutton, from Silverdale, was loyal to the brand, even if he could not keep the same bike.
"I got my first one aged about six and I had a Grifter, then a Sprinter Racing bike and a Raleigh Super Burner BMX," he said.
"It would be a Christmas thing. You'd give your parents a decent idea of what you wanted but it would still be a nice surprise on the day.
"Then you would take it out no matter what the weather, rain or snow.
"We were in West Bridgford then and I'd ride down the road, with my brother on his new bike, we'd ride to the car park and there would be all the other kids doing the same.
"They were great bikes, really well made.
"I have to say it - it's the end of an era."

title: From making friends to managing money: Students' advice for this year's freshers
description: BC News asked current students about the worries they had before arriving at university how they overcame them.
author: Grace Dean
content:
While they were excited to start university, students say they worried about budgeting, making friends and being homesick
You've got your A-level results and your university place has been confirmed.
But while you may be excited about exploring a new city, meeting new friends and studying a subject you love - you might also be a bit anxious about what comes next.
With a record number of 18-year-olds expected to start university this year, BBC News asked current students what advice they'd give to freshers feeling uncertain about the big changes ahead.
For Isaak Hewitt, moving to Cardiff for university - where he knew no-one - was a "completely blank slate".
The idea of meeting lots of new people for the first time since starting secondary school was nerve-racking he says, but Isaak made friends by talking to people he met at lectures and seminars. Now aged 20, Isaak says he was sometimes "terrified" trying to strike up conversations, but the fact everyone was studying English together gave them common ground.
He advises freshers to act confident - even if you're scared inside - and to put yourself out there.
Many people say making friends is one of their biggest worries about starting uni
As a commuter student in Nottingham, Grace Morrell was also worried about how she'd meet people, when others were making friends through their halls and student flats. Instead, Grace says she met new people by joining her student magazine, and the radio and theatre societies.
"A lot of my friendships come from putting myself out there and just doing what I love, which I found was a bit hard at times, especially when you don't know anyone," says Grace, 19.
'I worked really hard and it paid off': Elation, nerves and proud parents as students get results
Are the UK's top universities really 'hoovering up' students?
Lots of students try to connect with future coursemates and flatmates on social media before they start university, like Mustafa Dassu, 19, who says freshers' WhatsApp chats helped him make friends before he started at King's College London.
"Everyone was typing on them all the time between that period of results day and freshers' itself," Mustafa says, "and I met friends that I'm still in touch with a lot today."
"I really worried about having to be on my own," says Izzy Garcez, 20, who thought she would miss spending evenings with her family and having people to eat and watch TV with.
But in the end she wasn't as homesick as she'd anticipated.
"Realistically, you'll make friends so quickly at uni," Izzy says, "and you're going to get to a point where you realise 'I've not called my parents in a week', and you'll realise that suddenly you're not actually missing them anymore - or not missing them nearly as much."
Kieran says it's important to remember your maintenance loan has to last until the next instalment
Journalism student Kieran Miller was worried about money, but he compared student bank accounts and chose one that gave him a free 16-25 Railcard, and signed up for student discount schemes.
Everything you need to know about university costs
Though it might be exciting to see your first maintenance loan payment hit your bank account in one big lump sum, Kieran, 19, says you need to remember it has to last until the next instalment.
With the help of his mum, Kieran, from Swansea, made a provisional budget before moving away, but warns that it's easy to get caught up in the student experience and spend more than you planned to.
"When you start uni and you're living away from your family and you've got this new sense of freedom it was also really difficult to stay strict financially because you want to make mates with people," he says. "Someone might invite you to go for food or to go for a drink - and you're like, 'I don't really want to say no because this is a chance to connect with someone.'"
As well as student loans, most universities offer a variety of scholarships and bursaries, and it's worth checking whether you're eligible.
Many students balance classes and studying alongside part-time work, volunteering, sports clubs and societies.
Before starting her English and drama degree, Avery Hewitt, 19, worried about juggling studying with working and playing in a university band. She says speaking online to a student ambassador about the workload helped her manage her expectations.
Avery also advises new students to be realistic about their timetable and how much they can take on.
"I threw myself into everything in the first semester, which I quickly figured out was too much to handle," Avery says, "so I had to make responsible choices about what societies or club nights I needed to cut back on."
Pia switched from biochemistry to film and English
Even though your place is now confirmed, it's still not too late to change your mind. You can contact your university before you start to ask about changing course, or you can apply for courses at other universities through clearing.
After she started at the University of East Anglia, Pia Subong, 21, says she realised that biochemistry wasn't the right course for her and so switched to film and English.
If you're having doubts about whether the course is right for you, "you're having these feelings for a reason," Pia says.
Fatima says taking a gap year was the right decision for her
You can also take a gap year, as Fatima Qureshi, 19, from London did - because she wasn't sure which course she wanted to do or which career path she'd enjoy.
Fatima eventually decided to study law, but if she had chosen a course the year previously she'd likely have opted for biochemistry or pharmacy.
"It was the best thing I could have done," she says.
It's natural to feel anxious, according to Mel Kennedy, student wellbeing adviser at Ulster University, who says change "can be scary" and lots of people experience "fear of the unknown".
"For many students, starting university is the first time that they're stepping into a genuinely unknown environment," agrees Lindsay While, assistant director for student wellbeing and welfare at Teesside University.
"Many students do experience anxiety and uncertainty because it is such a major transition, but everybody's experience is completely different."
Universities offer a range of practical and wellbeing services, including budgeting advice, financial support, counselling and study support sessions. You can also reach out to the university if you need support before you start.
Some people told BBC News university had felt like the expected next step after sixth form or college. But Aashi Soni, 20, from Leicester, knew it wasn't right for her.
"Your college and sixth form don't really push you down that path [of apprenticeships] like they do with university and I found it really difficult," Aashi says. She turned down her university offers and took a gap year to find a suitable apprenticeship.
In the end, Aashi started a Level 6 degree apprenticeship in sales at Coca-Cola Europacific Partners. She says it has helped her grow in confidence, gain real-life experience while studying, and get mentoring.
Aashi and Meenu say university is often presented as the default option - but it wasn't right for them
Meenu Hettigama, 21, from Walsall began a creative media course after leaving school, but soon dropped out and applied for apprenticeships instead. She is now two years into a management degree apprenticeship at Amazon.
"University is not the only pathway," Meenu says, "even if maybe you think it's the most conventional or it is what your family want you to do."
You can search for apprenticeships on the UK government, Welsh government, Northern Ireland government and apprenticeships.scot websites. You can also find apprenticeships on sites like LinkedIn and Indeed and at apprenticeship recruitment events.

title: Children as young as nine hurt in growing number of e-scooter crashes
description: Three trauma centres - Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield - say they have treated nearly 500 casualties under the age of 16.
author: Michelle Roberts
content:
Some hospitals are seeing more and more children with injuries from e-scooters, a new review suggests , external .
Three trauma centres - Liverpool, Manchester and Sheffield - say they have treated 477 under-16s since 2019, with the number of cases per year rising from fewer than 10 in 2019 to nearly 150 in 2024.
The average age of those injured was 12, with the youngest nine. Hardly any were wearing helmets.
The emergency department doctors are calling for laws to better protect children. Currently in the UK, there is no legal age restriction, speed limit or safety equipment requirement for the estimated 1.2 million , external people who own private e-scooters.
Jacob Calland, pictured with his mother Carly Calland, was the passenger when the scooter collided with a BMW car
Some e-scooters have a "turbo mode" setting, meaning they can reach speeds of around 28mph.
Recently, a UK teenager using one of these crashed and killed his 14-year-old friend on a busy road - one of 59 deaths involving e-scooters in the UK to date.
Jacob Calland, who was a passenger on the back, suffered irreversible brain injuries when it was struck by a BMW car in Wythenshawe, Manchester, on 19 March 2025.
Manchester Crown Court heard the teenager driving the e-scooter also sustained serious injuries, including a bleed on the brain and numerous bone fractures.
And Det Con Steve Pennington from Greater Manchester Police's Serious Collision Investigation Unit stressed e-scooters were not harmless toys and could lead to horrific consequences when used by inexperienced riders.
Most of the incidents in Manchester, Liverpool and Sheffield involved private e-scooters, often on public roads, pavements or footpaths, despite that being illegal.
Private e-scooters are meant only for use on private land, with the owner's permission.
Half of the children injured were aged between 10 and 13. Nearly two-thirds were boys.
Most injuries were sustained by the rider - only 5% were pedestrians that had been hit by an e-scooter - and the most common cause was falling off the e-scooter.
Around 11% were collisions with a vehicle, which was often linked to more serious injuries.
Injuries to the arms and legs were the most common, followed by head or facial injuries.
The doctors say tougher laws are urgently needed. Helmet use is not mandatory in the UK, unlike some other countries.
Some have described the private e-scooter situation in the UK as the "Wild West" with few following any rules.
The researchers told the Emergency Medicine Journal that schools, local councils, youth groups and road safety campaigns all have a role to play.
"Clearly, reporting these accidents is important to influence and change policy, but there must also be an onus on retailers to clearly advise customers of the law, and policymakers to regulate private e-scooters, such as with speed limiters, or mandate helmet use," they say.
To legally rent an e-scooter in the UK, which can be used on roads and cycle lanes, you must be at least 16 and hold a full or provisional driving licence, and the rental company must provide appropriate insurance. Rental e-scooters typically have a limited top speed of around 15mph.
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: "These are concerning findings, and our thoughts are with anyone who has been injured on our roads.
"It is illegal for private e-scooters to be used on roads, pavements or in other public spaces, including by under 16s, and we're bringing forward new laws to make their use safe and legal, including consulting on requirements like helmets."

title: Sarwar ministerial role sees promotion of another Starmer critic
description: Months after calling on Keir Starmer to quit, the Scottish Labour leader is set to become a minister in Burnham's government, the BBC's political editor writes.
author: Chris Mason
content:
The imminent appointment of the Scottish Labour leader Anas Sarwar to Andy Burnham's government, via a seat in the House of Lords, sees the promotion of another key figure in the downfall of Sir Keir Starmer as prime minister.
When Sarwar said publicly, back in February, that Sir Keir should stand down, it was a moment of colossal jeopardy for the now former prime minister.
It looked, briefly, like it might bring about an immediate and irrevocable collapse in his authority. Then, one after another, cabinet ministers posted their support for him on social media.
As I wrote at the time , missives of public loyalty from cabinet ministers towards a prime minister shouldn't be newsworthy and they only become so when the opposite seems feasible.
Now, five months on, Sarwar will be swapping Holyrood for Westminster and becoming a minister.
He will be joining Miatta Fahnbulleh in government, the new energy secretary in Burnham's cabinet, who was the first government minister to resign from Sir Keir's administration saying she had lost faith in him .
Also around the cabinet table, the new Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who let it be known in what turned out to be Sir Keir's final weeks in office that he had suggested to him that he ought to accept that his time was up.
It is also worth mentioning too John Healey, who resigned as defence secretary, and Wes Streeting, who resigned as health secretary towards the end of Sir Keir's time in Downing Street, are now in prominent roles in Burnham's cabinet as chancellor and defence secretary respectively.
This is the backdrop to comments from Steve Reed, the former communities secretary and doughty defender of Sir Keir at some of his moments of most intense peril.
Reed wrote to Burnham as he left government and said: "I hope those who did not show loyalty to Keir will now show it to you. I am proud that I acted with integrity at every step over the turbulent past few months."
There is, right now, as you would expect, overwhelming support for Burnham among Labour MPs.
But these public remarks from Reed are an indicator of the wells of private hurt and anger created by the events of recent days, weeks and months.
It is a reminder that, of course, all the folk you are reading and hearing about are human beings who have each keenly felt the tremors of uncertainty in recent months â?? and depending on their circumstances, outlook, instincts and judgement, have arrived at differing conclusions and decisions about how to act.
The public intervention of Darren Jones, another loyal lieutenant of the former prime minister, taking a swipe at the funding of the government's planned cut in VAT on domestic electricity bills should be seen in this context too.
Labour's switch from one leader to another was less drawn out and dramatic than it might have been, as there was neither a formal leadership challenge to Sir Keir, nor more than one contender to replace him once he had announced his intention to go.
But it is also true that what we have witnessed the climax of this week, and the build up to for months on end, is not cost or pain free for a political party and some of that is manifesting itself now â?? and may still do for some time.
